speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUSPENSION OF SATURDAY SITTINGS FOR TWO WEEKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house is aware, on May 8, 1961, as reported at page 4494 of Hansard, I made a motion with regard to the extended sittings of the house, as follows:
That on Saturday, May 13,	1961, and every
Saturday thereafter until the end of the session the order of business and procedure shall be as for Thursday, a government day.
I think there has been general agreement that a continuation for the next two weeks, in any event, of Saturday sittings would not be necessary. We have to think of the welfare of those connected with the administration of the house. Discussions have taken place among representatives of the government, the opposition and the third party in this matter, and I am very happy to say that an agreement has been arrived at.
We are now dealing with a most important matter, the question of external affairs, to be followed by the estimates of defence, and the house has shown an anxiety and a desire to proceed with these two very important matters without delay. Under normal circumstances on Monday and Tuesday there would be a motion to go into supply in order to open up the other four departments that have not yet been opened up. There has been agreement that the motion will be made and the departments will be opened up on Monday without debate, thereby enabling the house to proceed unbrokenly with the business before us, which concerns all of us. The attention paid by hon. members of the house and the manner in which the debate was conducted yesterday indicate the desire of all to do everything possible to meet the situation that we face.
In view of that agreement with respect to going into supply I move, seconded by Mr. Churchill:
That the operation of the provision of the resolution adopted by the house on April 24 last concerning Saturday sittings, which reads as follows:
"Saturday: 11.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m.; 2.30 to 6.00 p.m." be suspended for the next two Saturday
sittings and that when the house adjourns today and on Friday next it shall stand adjourned until the following Monday at eleven o'clock a.m.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subtopic: SUSPENSION OF SATURDAY SITTINGS FOR TWO WEEKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the procedure
which the Prime Minister has outlined and the motion which has just been put to the house is quite agreeable to us. Indeed, it has been the subject of discussion among all parties in the house. The reading of the motion, Mr. Speaker, reminds us that it was as far back as April 24 when we changed our rules to permit these long hours, including Saturdays, and that in turn reminds us that during this time the house was sitting, the staff and officials who serve the house have been working under very great pressure indeed, and very effectively in spite of the pressure.
I think, among other things, this motion will serve to relieve that pressure. In the terms in which it has been put before the house it will not, I think, slow up or postpone any of our deliberations. Perhaps, by giving us a little more time on Saturday, if we are not engaged in other activities on Saturday afternoons, it will permit us to prepare for the debates in the subsequent week. We are entirely in favour of it.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF SATURDAY SITTINGS FOR TWO WEEKS
speechtext:
The
members of this group wholeheartedly support the proposal made by the Prime Minister for this change in our procedure at the present time. We believe it will do something toward promoting the efficiency of parliament by giving members a little more time to do the things that are necessary. We believe it indicates some rather belated consideration of the staff, and it will also be to the welfare of the gentlemen and others who are members of the fourth estate.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUSPENSION OF SATURDAY SITTINGS FOR TWO WEEKS
speechtext: Perhaps the further matter mentioned by the Prime Minister might be made the subject of a unanimous order at this time so there will be no uncertainty on Monday when the sixth supply motion is called. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the end of the first part of the session the hon. member for Kootenay West put to me the following question:

In view of the minister's statement in the house on July 11 that the civil service commission has followed the policy of granting regular leave to full time civil servants only, would the minister care to comment on the fact that as far back as ten years ago the civil service commission advertised positions or part time stenographers in the Ottawa papers and offered sick leave and holiday benefits ?
This is my answer. In my statement on July 11, 1961, regarding paid leave for part time employees, to the effect that the government has followed the policy of granting regular leave only to full time civil servants,
I should have made a distinction between persons regularly employed part time on a set time basis of so many hours per day, or for example on a half time basis, as opposed to persons employed sporadically from time to time on what is known as a casual basis.
In the former cases it is the policy of the government, and this includes the civil service commission, to grant regular leave-vacation, sick and special-on a basis which is scaled proportionately to the number of hours worked. It is true, therefore, that a half time stenographer receives one half the normal leave credits. She would, therefore, receive three weeks annual leave, or fifteen days, but would be paid for half her fifteen days only or, in total, one half of fifteen days' pay. On the other hand, in those departments which have employees engaged on a sporadic or casual basis, it is not the practice to grant leave benefits.
As already reported on July 11, this whole matter is now being studied by the civil service commission.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure all members of this house feel that yesterday's debate was a splendid one, conducted in a mood of great seriousness in keeping with the urgency and gravity of this hour in mankind's history. Naturally most attention was given to Berlin, where the iron curtain has now become a physical thing symbolic of those great, deep differences existing today in respect of the political and civil rights of man.
I was, nevertheless, impressed with the fact that a good many members gave thought to other areas of the world as well. Sometimes we tend to concentrate on the major and immediate crisis and allow another one to develop with which we have to deal at a later time. I thought the Secretary of State for External Affairs made one of his greatest speeches. In a brief, simple and straightforward statement he set the record straight on NATO, on the commonwealth and especially on the United Nations and Canada's support of and faith in that great organization.
If I may be pardoned a personal expression I may say that the president of the United Nations assembly is today in my constituency in the province of Prince Edward Island. If it were not for this important debate and my duties in the House of Commons, I would be there to greet this distinguished man as he comes to that most beautiful part of Canada to discuss today's most important events and, I hope, to get a little rest in our beautiful province. Like the Secretary of State for External Affairs I, too, hope that the U.S.S.R. has not lost its sensitivity to world opinion.
As the Charlottetown Guardian said the other day:
It poses a new threat to world survival which the U.N. must deal with at its regular general assembly session this month; and therein lies the last hope that the reaction to its appalling significance will cause a change in Kremlin strategy before it is too late.
All of us are deeply concerned lest war descend upon us, for we know its terrors. We know how utterly it would destroy us all. In many ways it is this awareness of the awfulness of war that makes diplomacy so difficult. There is always the danger of forsaking strength and steadiness in our horror of what may happen, and these are the essential ingredients of successful diplomacy. I noted that the hon. member for Kootenay West said that no Berliners would be left alive if the issue 90205-6-512
were settled by war, and God knows that is true. But how long would freedom itself live if we gave in in the face of the threats that emanate from the Soviet union and continued to cave in in future confrontations?
I am always a little uneasy when I hear the expression, is Berlin worth fighting for? Is this remote and distant city worth pushing the crisis to its ultimate? None of us thinks it would be a good idea to fight because the old idea of war is completely out of the picture these days. Yet I can never forget those inane utterances of Neville Chamberlain when he referred to Czechoslovakia as "that remote and unknown country". We cannot think in these terms any more. Of course we must make every possible exertion to avoid war. Indeed, I think the minister was right when he said we will have to exert ourselves more than we have heretofore. Perhaps it is my Calvinism that causes me to be most impressed when he calls for great physical and moral courage. I think it is very appropriate to the needs of the present day and hour. I think we will have to prepare ourselves for a harder road. We should be ready to recognize that, as the minister said, perhaps we have had enough of the soft life.
In my maiden speech in the house I quoted a brief, succinct passage from that wonderful newspaper the Christian Science Monitor, in which it was stated:
We prefer a tax cut we think-to a satellite or a missile-until the Russians have one. And then the heart searching begins.
Well, soul searching and heart searching were never more needed than in this moment in mankind's history.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly about an area which I have discussed during external affairs debates in previous sessions. I was honoured to be one of the Canadian observer delegation to the special inter-American economic and social conference held in Punta del Este. I am deeply grateful to the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government for appointing me as a member of that observer delegation. My status was such that I had to observe with both eyes, because the delegation itself was an observer group. I should like to express my personal thanks to the leader of that delegation, the Associate Minister of National Defence, for the many courtesies shown me. He gave the delegation splendid leadership and I was proud of the fact that in all his contacts he made a great impression and won friendship for Canada.
I think the visits of Canadian leaders to South America are most important. While there I heard many references to the recent visit of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as well as to the visit of the previous

Supply-External Affairs secretary of state for external affairs, the late Dr. Sidney Smith. I hope the Prime Minister himself will be able to go down to that part of the world in which he is held in such high regard by the people who stand for the great things for which he has stood throughout the whole of his public career.
In today's world the southern hemisphere is vital, not so much in this direct kind of explosive contact we discuss when dealing with Berlin but in that socio-political economic contest in which Mr. Khrushchev has promised to bury us. In that struggle the lands and peoples south of the equator are tremendously important. I think they are aware of the importance which they now hold, and they are doing much to help themselves. They realize, I believe, that they are at the crossroads in their historic development.
I havev said before, and I reiterate, that this government deserves compliments and commendation for what it has done to strengthen our ties with Latin America. New missions have been opened, and now we are about to be represented in every single nation in the Latin American world. The appointment of the observer delegation to Punta del Este was most deeply appreciated. I heard that on every hand. The new contacts that are developing, the visits that are taking place, are all to the good. I think it is in our interest to do more of this. I believe we must press for closer and closer contacts, especially in the technical and academic fields.
I was very pleased with the references made by the hon. member for Fort William in this connection. He was almost born in one of the Latin American states and might have become a deputy in Brazil had he stayed there a little longer. Last session I spoke of the beginning of the Latin American institute at King's College, Halifax, the oldest university in Canada. There is great hope in this, for there is a fine program developing there. I should like to see a program of scholarships similar to that in which Canada gave such great leadership in connection with the commonwealth scholarship plan.
There is one more question to which reference has already been made in this debate, and that is membership in the organization of American states. For a long time, indeed for 15 years or more, I have held that Canada would be well advised to become a member of this hemispheric association. I am more strongly convinced than ever that this is the right course. There was one time, many years ago, when we were not wanted. Of course we were technically ineligible then.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
This situation has long since passed and, publicly and privately, we have been invited to take our place, to occupy that vacant chair which someone in a spirit of optimism had actually built in 1912 when the Pan-American Union building was opened in Washington. We have had the invitation from President Kennedy. However, some years before, that distinguished American Senator Vandenberg issued an invitation in very fine words which now come to my mind. He said:
By every rule of righteousness she Is eligible to this association. By every rule of reason we should wish her here. I should welcome the final and total new world unity which will be nobly dramatized when the twenty second chair is filled and our continental brotherhood is complete from the Arctic circle to Cape Horn.
Among the Latin Americans I was privileged to meet at the conference at Punta del Este I found complete unanimity in the view that Canada would be most welcome. They would be very happy to have us take our place among this group. I am not the first to report with respect to this unanimity. This has been reported by much abler persons than I, and notably by the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself in recent statements.
Should Canada join? What will we get out of it? Perhaps we should also ask what we can contribute to it. I observed that the minister spoke yesterday about the essential need of continuing the ingredient of idealism in our foreign policy. We would greatly strengthen the organization of American states, the oldest collective security organization in the world today. We have much in common with the Latin American countries now forming its membership. We have a colonial past. Our colonial problems and difficulties were different from theirs and we met them in a different way, but suffice it to say that we had our problems and dealt with them in our own way, finally emerging with independent status. Another similarity lies in the fact that our country was settled by Europeans many years ago, and we have close continuing ties with the European continent.
We, like many countries in Latin America, have great natural resources requiring a major effort to effect their development. We have, however, something which not all and indeed not many Latin American states have. We have a long record of political stability. Indeed, between the years 1935 and 1957 I thought we were becoming too stable in our political life. We have a history of settled, orderly government. We also have technical know-how. Canada is a country with a mature economy and an advanced technology. We

have the very things which the nations south of the Rio Grande require so desperately in these difficult times.
I wish to deal now with the advantages that could accrue from our joining. This is no place to discuss the prospects of improving our trade with Latin America, but let me say I am firmly convinced that there is a great potential for expansion in that part of the world. As another advantage I should mention that we would strengthen the western alliance by strengthening the organization of American states. We would improve our contacts and relations with people who wish to be our friends. During the few years I served as a delegate to the United Nations I became thoroughly convinced of the basic friendship between Canadians and Latin Americans. That friendship is extremely important, especially at the United Nations in the light of what has happened with respect to the membership pattern there.
The old arguments against our joining are now passe. There were those who used to argue that our joining would work to the detriment of the commonwealth in some way, that the two were incompatible. The commonwealth has now developed into a new form. There is greater freedom among the members! I think it not impossible that before too long we could have two commonwealth states in the organization of American states. The British West Indies federation might well be a member of both bodies in the very near future.
There is another argument which always disturbs me. Some have argued that there is a danger in joining, that we might find ourselves having to side with the United States against the Latin Americans or side with the Latin Americans against the United States. Someone yesterday in the debate used the word "subservience". I have witnessed the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his dealings with some delegations at the United Nations. While I should not like to use the word "stubbornness" in relation to the hon. gentleman, I have never found him guilty of subservience, nor have I seen him hesitate to disagree when he thought it was proper and in Canada's interest to do so.
The Prime Minister of this country needs no suggestions concerning the proper exercise of Canada's independent role in world affairs. The Prime Minister set the record straight in that famous Dartmouth College speech which he made shortly after he became Prime Minister. The argument of subservience is out of date. Indeed it is contemptible. Canada can differ when it feels there is a point of difference. We are free to agree not because the 90205-6-512J
Supply-External Affairs United States is rich and powerful and we are afraid to disagree, but because in the issues that face the world today we find ourselves in agreement with United States due to the fact that it is on the side of right.
I heard this thought brilliantly expressed by my friend the hon. member for Parkdale when he spoke in my constituency not long ago. Sometimes I feel there is too much anti-Americanism on the part of the would-be intellectuals of the country, the Gamaliels of the press gallery and the general reportorial group. Often this negative sentiment is passed off as Canadian nationalism. I believe this is scarcely the time to indulge in anti-Americanism. It is very easy to find flaws in the record of a country which bears the burdens of world leadership. In the nineteenth century the favourite intellectual exercise was twisting the lion's tail; now it is plucking the feathers from the eagle.
I think these dark days are hardly suited for indulging in such activities. We have to recognize that while we have long since reached the stage where we are capable of asserting and do assert our independence, when the chips are down Canada and the United States are on the same team. I shudder when I hear Canadians equate the aims of the U.S.S.R. with those of the U.S.A., and with a fine impartiality say "A plague on both your houses; we will step on the United States' corns and Russia's corns, too".
There were bad days in the relations of the United States with her southern neighbours. I suppose they were at their worst at the time of Theodore Roosevelt and reached their highest level under a United States president of the same name. The United States has learnt much during the course of its relations with its Latin American neighbours and during the course of its relations with Canada as well. President Kennedy in his recent program, alianza para el progresso, advanced an imaginative, forward looking program designed to improve relations through united leadership as opposed to United States supremacy. Yesterday the Associate Minister of National Defence described the tremendous contributions the United States has been prepared to make-in raw, physical terms, a contribution of $20 billion-to assist Latin America, which perhaps with some justification has felt a little neglected in recent years as Washington has had forced upon it crisis after crisis to which it has had to give its immediate attention.
I was tremendously impressed by the performance of Mr. Dillon, the chief United States delegate at the inter-American con-

Supply-External Affairs ference. He began his opening speech by quoting a statement of the Cuban liberator, Jose Marti, who said:
We Americans are one in origin, in hope and in danger.
Mr. Dillon went on to say:
We meet today in fulfilment of the concept and brought together by our common origin, fired by our common hopes, determined to conquer our common dangers.
Although there are great differences between us and many of the peoples of Latin America and indeed of the United States, we have so much in common that we cannot say, we dare not say, that what happens there does not affect nor concern us because verily it does. As ambassador Adlai Stevenson said:
We cannot look for strong brothers in arms against a common enemy as long as any of our fellow American nations are sapped by stagnation and social decay.
Or as the Associate Minister of National Defence expressed it yesterday:
Our fate will be a better one if the fate of our neighbours in Latin America is also a better one.
To advance, to strengthen this area will make for a better world and strengthen the causes to which we have dedicated ourselves. Happily we are in a position to help. I am convinced that we will do so on an ever increasing scale. It has not been the Canadian attitude to fail in our responsibilities to the world.
In this particular part of the world to which I have been giving my attention in these last few minutes I think the opportunity is great, the challenge is great, but happily we are able to meet both. I would hope we shall go further in this direction than we already have gone, and that here will be one area in which this struggle in the future, if we have a future, will be resolved in the right way for the right causes and on behalf of the right people.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following the recent incidents which occurred in Berlin and the resumption of nuclear tests by the U.S.S.R., the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) informed us yesterday of the various measures which the government has decided to take, such as increased military forces in Canada and Europe, the establishment of a recruiting and training program to facilitate civil defence in our country.
Quite contrary to his usual optimistic mood, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) yesterday summarized his slightly pessimistic opinion in these words: We are on the brink of nuclear war. It still remains to be seen to what extent the steps [Mr. Macquarrie.l
taken by the government and the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will satisfy public opinion in Canada.
At the end of the speech she made yesterday, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) expressed some disappointment in the very limited review made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I am inclined to share her disappointment since I feel the time would have been most appropriate yesterday for the Canadian government's spokesman to state very clearly the government's policy concerning external affairs, in view of the present problems.
In my opinion, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) brilliantly stated yesterday the views of the official opposition. He made various suggestions to the government and I hope the latter will take them into serious consideration. I think-in fact, I am quite sure -that the government will appreciate the spirit in which those suggestions were made because, at the end of his speech, the hon. member for Essex East called for united action on the part of all Canadian political parties to deal with the serious problem we are faced with concerning national security.
I am sure that his appeal will meet the approval of all Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, the present tension over Berlin does not result from a new problem. Last year, a few colleagues and I had the opportunity of following the deliberations of the NATO parliamentary association and we visited NATO's Canadian military bases and refugee camps in West Berlin. Following that trip and the talks we had with west Berlin local authorities, we had the impression that the Berlin question would one day give rise to the tension we experience today. That problem is not the only important one on which the east and west are divided, but it is definitely the most crucial and capital one; indeed, if there is a strategical point in the world where the western countries must not retreat, it is in west Berlin. The western world's position concerning Germany and Berlin has been clearly stated and it must be forcefully reiterated. I quite agree with the government on this point, but once that position is taken, nothing should stand in the way of negotiations even if a solution of the problem seems hard to find today because of the Soviets' uncompromisingness and insincerity.
In fact, what is the problem? There are in Berlin 2.5 million Germans who are anticommunists and whose sympathies, culture and economic ties lie with the western world.

Because of their affection for democratic countries, I feel that we have an undeniable obligation to see that they are not overtaken against their will by the communists. But in spite of its importance, I think that we can consider the Berlin crisis as a symbolic factor in this fight between eastern and western ideologies.
Therefore, that is the reason why I say that the present issue is much more important than the Berlin and German problems. Let us never forget that if the communists claim to be the defenders of a world wide doctrine, should we weaken on the Berlin issue, the Russians' hunger would not be satisfied.
Communism aims to engulf the yellow race, the black race and the white race-Asia, Africa, Europe and America. The final aim of communism, let us never forget it, is not merely a local victory or a continental victory, but complete domination-communist dominion over the world.
In addition, I feel that if we consider and think over what happened since the end of the last war we will be realistic enough to admit that, and that being admitted, there are two questions we can ask ourselves. What is the position the western world should take in the light of such a crisis, especially after the resumption of nuclear testing? Should we take a rigid stand on the Berlin issue and keep our ground firmly, even though we may run the risk of starting a war? Second, what position should a country like Canada take when faced with problems of a scope much beyond its strength?
Before answering the first question, I should like to read a few lines of a speech delivered by Mr. Khrushchev a few months ago-less than a year ago-before the supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R., on January 14, 1960. It will be seen from this statement which seems very clear that even Mr. Khrushchev admits that nuclear warfare between two countries who have nuclear weapons is meaningless. I quote:
Let us suppose that a state or a group of states succeed in preparing and launching a surprise attack against a power which has nuclear weapons and rockets. Could the aggressors, by a single blow of the nuclear weapons, destroy all the installations for the launching of rockets within the borders of the attacked power, even if they succeeded in keeping their attack undetected? Certainly not.
The state who is suddenly attacked, assuming it is a large enough one, will always have a possibility to retaliate with equally powerful blows. We take into consideration the fact that our country is surrounded by foreign military bases; that is why we are installing our launching sites in such a way as to insure a second and a third line of defence. The fact that our territory is enormously large makes it possible for us to decentralise our launching sites and to hide them well. We are building a system by which it will
Supply-External Affairs be possible whenever one of our answering devices is put out of order, to operate a second one and to hit our objectives from reserve positions.
And Mr. Khrushchev concludes as follows:
All this is indeed enough to cool off any psychically normal person, and the men who are responsible to the world and who have its destiny at heart.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure no sensible man would think a nuclear war might mean victory for the victor, in the sense given to that term until now. And, in the light of the passage I read a moment ago, it seems that Khrushchev himself has understood that the introduction and use of nuclear weapons have utterly upset the very notion of war. That quotation from Khrushchev's words is, in my opinion, additional proof of the fact that, in order to manage to survive along with communism, we must negotiate from strength, this being the only language he can understand.
Does that mean that, after having clearly established our positions, as in the case of West Berlin, we must uphold them without entering into negotiations? Of course, that would be a very serious mistake. I was listening, some time ago, to a remarkable interview on "Close Up", of Mr. Walter Lippmann, an American newspaperman who is much listened to and has had several talks with Mr. Khrushchev. On that program, the following question was put to Mr. Lippmann: Now that the die is cast over West Berlin, that both sides have clearly established their positions, what should the west do about the German problem? And Mr. Lippmann replied: (Text):
Well I think that the next step is one which involves a change in our basic approach to the German problem. We have taken the line conventionally that everything in Berlin is as good as it could be from our point of view, that any change in this situation of Berlin would be for the worse, therefore we must stand firm and stand pat. That's Dr. Adenauer's view. Change nothing. Fight-threaten to fight if anything is changed.
Later, Mr. Lippmann, though admitting that we should not basically change our position as to west Berlin, says that as a result we are in a disadvantageous position. He goes on to say:
We should take the position that the freedom of Berlin, in the sense of their ability to govern themselves, to live their own life, to keep their physical and economic and spiritual and political contacts with the western world, cannot be touched. We won't negotiate about that. But the legal basis and the statutory rights that go with that are negotiable. They never were negotiated. The thing is all a clutter of catch-can things made by generals and various people and we ought to say to them- I would like to see the position of saying to Khrushchev, "We don't like Berlin the way it is; we want to improve it, and if you can negotiate with us an improvement we'd be very interested."

Supply-External Affairs (Translation)
Negotiations should therefore certainly be pursued, even if the main problem cannot be settled. Following an agreement, it would be possible to meet and settle the corollaries to the main question and we also, perhaps, might ask for the status quo to be maintained in the Berlin matter, even if it were only for one year.
I even think that, in this attempt at negotiating so as to relieve world tensions, the western nations should take more considerable and marked action than they have in the past. We should prove to the whole world and convince more particularly the non-committed nations, that the western countries want to solve their problems with the east in one way and one place only, that is, at a conference table.
I think we can agree, and there is nothing wrong with doing so, that our propaganda has not always been a happy one in this respect. We know that the western countries have no imperialistic views and do not aim at conquest, but I think that our propaganda has too often been deplorable, which gave rise to some doubts in the minds of too many people, more particularly in the non-committed countries, and those doubts should not exist considering the generosity of the western countries, first of all the United States and Canada.
I believe that Canada can play an important part in this respect among its allies. Let us recall this country's action in the Suez crisis. The former secretary of state for external affairs, who is today the Leader of the Opposition, had, on behalf of a sovereign Canada, taken a position, unimpaired by any inferiority complex. We may recall that results were in keeping with our attitude, and that considerable prestige was earned by our country. This answers in a way the second question I was asking earlier today.
What attitude should be taken by a country like Canada? I believe that we should as we did for Suez, take any position which to our mind, could promote world peace, considering not only the higher interests of Canada but of all the free nations.
As far as the renewal of nuclear tests is concerned, we should obviously condemn the U.S.S.R. without reserve, as we must also regret, if not blame, the American attitude in this matter, though the American nuclear tests are to be made underground
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
and will therefore not endanger the life of individuals by radioactive fall-out.
To my mind, there is no people in this world, including the Russian people, who would favour those tests. When the Soviets decided to break the lull of a three year agreement in order to continue their nuclear tests, we had an excellent opportunity to expose that country to world opinion, but I think this should have been done before the only proper court, that is, the United Nations.
This is a field where a country like Canada can play an important part. But in addition the government should have a clearly defined policy on this issue. It may be difficult to blame others for making those tests when it is possible that the results they obtain may find a use in our own country by the stocking of nuclear warheads on our launching bases. Therefore we should have a clearly defined policy in connection with the use of nuclear warheads. In my opinion, this procrastination on the part of the government prevents us to a certain extent from playing our due part on the world scene in that respect.
Mr. Chairman, here in Canada we have regard for the basic principles which are essential to men of all countries if they want to develop harmoniously and live in an atmosphere of freedom. Our way of life is essentially dependent on other spiritual values not on atheistic materialism.
In his speech, Mr. Khrushchev as I said a moment ago also made the following statement on which I want to comment. Mr. Khrushchev said a few months ago before the supreme Soviet:
The U.S.S.R. will produce more coal, more steel and more oil than the United States within ten years from now.
Commenting on that statement, Mr. Spaak, the former secretary general of NATO had the following statement to make:
I do not believe in totalitarianism nor in historical materialism. There is only one thing we can do and it is to remain true to our essential principles and to accept within our countries as well as outside our boundaries the consequences of that loyalty.
And what he added was actually the truth:
The problem is not to know who produces the most, it is to know what one does with the wealth thus gained, what kind of society one organizes and what sort of hope is given to the people.
It is here, Mr. Chairman, that democracies have a huge advantage over communism. That freedom of action and thought that we are demanding for the men of all countries

and all races, explains the greater economic failure of the soviets, a failure and a fiasco they are unable to hide. That is why hundreds of thousands of men, women and children, at the risk of their lives, want to cross communist borders to enjoy an atmosphere of freedom within the western democracies.
I think that there lies one of the capital issues connected with the Berlin problem. That is why we must be ready to enter any proposed negotiations and also at the same time maintain a strong stand on the principles at stake, because this issue, let us never forget it, is mortgaging the future generations to come. Therefore we must do all in our power to save the sacred heritage we shall transmit to those who will follow in our footsteps.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF DIPLOMATIC MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fifteenth session of the United Nations opened in an atmosphere of tension and controversy resulting from the presence of the leaders of the two opposite blocs who wanted to bring forward before the general assembly all the problems that the international community must face today. Colonialism, nuclear tests and disarmament have been some of the main issues which have contributed to sow among the delegations a fever of threats and provocations that could imperil the peace and security of nations.
Fortunately, free nations had state leaders who, with energy and frankness, have unmasked the contradictory and ironical stands of the leaders of the satellite countries who seemed to have undertaken to sabotage the fifteenth meeting at all costs.
Among these courageous leaders, I should like to mention the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) who, on that occasion, made a speech indicating clearly to our allies how we must reply to the leaders of the countries under the communist regime and how we must successfully defend the philosophy of the nations anxious to live in a true democracy. That day, we were proud to be Canadians and to be governed by a leader with such distinction on the international scene.
The fifteenth session was also characterized by the entry of seventeen new nations into the organization. That was a political revolution with hardly any precedents in history. This sudden eruption, on the international scene, of a great many African countries, in full economic, social, cultural and psychological transformation, will bring about a
Supply-External Affairs radical change in political data and definitely influence the evolution of the rest of humanity. By asking for the recognition of their prerogatives and the granting of the status of sovereign countries, these newly created nations immediately indicated that they were determined to play an important part on the international scene.
While I was at the United Nations, I had the opportunity of working in close co-operation with the representatives of those new countries and I soon realized the importance of their presence within the international community.
In my opinion, the immediate consequences of their presence are the following:
1.	The number of small powers has increased with the result that the latter have made new efforts to unite in a spirit of cooperation to discuss their common problems at the diplomatic level. That does not necessarily mean that the presence of a solid bloc composed exclusively of African countries was felt at the United Nations, but the discussion of certain problems most definitely took on different aspects because of certain new characteristics brought by those new African countries.
2.	The presence of those new nations also had an influence on the activities and the procedure of the general assembly, because it was difficult to forecast the fate of a resolution due to an increased number of votes which could be cast in favour of the east or the west. The results of the vote on the membership of communist China is an indisputable example.
I should now like to say a word about the French-speaking African countries. Of the 28 African countries which achieved independence, 17 were former French colonies and 14 of those 17 countries gained their sovereignty in 1960. It goes without saying that the importance of those states may seem secondary from the points of view of population and economics, but it should not be forgotten that each of these new states has a seat at the United Nations assembly, can cast its vote and express its views on all international problems. Most of the Frenchspeaking African nations which were given their independence in 1960 are small countries whose population varies from 1 to 5 million. They are still getting assistance from France and have signed with the latter mutual aid and assistance treaties in the commercial and economic fields.

Supply-External Affairs
All those states are faced with urgent problems and Canada, as a bilingual country, must absolutely look into their needs and offer them a charitable and brotherly hand.
Last June, I went to Ruanda-Urundi as a member of a United Nations judiciary mission; I met with the aboriginal people of that country and I acquired a first-hand knowledge of their difficulties. I spoke with African leaders who expressed their fears about the future of those countries. Even though the Belgian authorities have carried out extensive material realizations in that territory under trusteeship, those people will still be in great need after they have achieved independence. In my opinion, the most urgent problem is the establishment of an administrative machinery. Africa's future depends on the training of its public officials, teachers, doctors, civil engineers and technicians of all kinds. From the point of view of education, we must strive to help those countries train enlightened leaders by developing education at the high school and university level. It is here that outside help will be necessary; it will include the provision of an ever increasing number of teachers and the establishment of scholarships for the formation of an elite capable of ensuring Africa's future.
The African leaders greeted with enthusiasm and gratefulness the Canadian government's decision to help financially the French-speaking countries of Africa.
You undoubtedly recall, Mr. Chairman, that on April 24, 1961, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) announced that the government was setting up a training assistance program for the benefit of French-speaking African states, by providing grants of $300,000 a year.
On that occasion, the Secretary of State for External Affairs had this to say as recorded on page 3930 of Hansard:
The countries to which the scheme would be directed are vitally preoccupied with the serious task of improving their educational facilities and with expanding educational opportunities for their peoples. They have repeatedly expressed their need for scholarships abroad for French-speaking students and for French-speaking teachers in their own countries. Because of our genuine interest in their welfare and progress and because we share a common language with these new states, Canada is in a unique position to render the type of assistance required. It is therefore the intention of the government to ask parliament to appropriate the funds necessary for this purpose once details have been worked out with the provincial educational authorities.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier), congratulating the government on this move, added the following which appears on page 3931 of Hansard:
[Mr. Asselin.3
In addition, I am particularly glad that the government has decided to confer with provincial authorities regarding the program it intends to submit.
However, I was sorry to learn recently, Mr. Chairman, that the Quebec government had not yet given any answer to the offer made by the federal government.
If there is a government that should support such a proposal, it is the Quebec government, the source of French culture in our country. I urge therefore the government to renew its offer to the Quebec government and, if need be, to remind that government of its responsibilities as concerns African aid.
I congratulate Canada for having shown leadership in this field because already the communists are launching a psychological attack in an effort to convince the new African states to join the communist ideology.
Our ambassador in Paris, Mr. Pierre Du-puy, reminded us of it last fall following a goodwill tour he made on behalf of Canada in those African countries when he said:
Communist propaganda constantly reminds Africans that in 1917 Russia was an underdeveloped country and that it took less than 50 years to make it into one of the most modern powers. Then why not follow its example?
Mr. Chairman, they also claim that the western parliamentary system is the result of a century of evolution and that it could not provide young and vigorous states with the authority, the decisiveness and the efficiency they need. Finally, they use the old and too well known slogan about colonialism. The degree of penetration of those arguments varies according to the intellectual and political maturity of the listeners. It is easy to influence certain African people with well illustrated pamphlets and periodicals. In Ruanda-Urundi I myself have seen some of the pamphlets illustrating industrial, agricultural, social and cultural progress made in the U.S.S.R. and communist China.
Youth in particular receives special consideration from those groups. No opportunity is lost of recruiting the most intelligent and understanding minds to take them on organized tours of communist countries. Thousands of scholarships are offered to students and others of those emerging countries. It was for them that the friendship university was recently founded in Moscow.
So, I urgently call on all freedom loving peoples to assist Africa before it gives in to communist pressure. It is true that Africa's future will require all kinds of capital but, still more, it will depend on the benevolent understanding of its problems by its genuine friends. The worst mistake, we are told time

and time again, would be to try to transform the African continent into a new America or Russia.
Africa, as we know, has a personality of its own, an originality richly endowed with human virtues. External contributions will be valuable to it to the extent that they will allow it to develop its own consciousness and reveal itself to the world at large.
As Mr. Dupuy also said, Africa is showing us the marvellous phenomenon of having survived in the midst of a turmoil of creative and destructive forces, of vegetal and animal forces, as are no more to be found anywhere else on our planet. But it did more than survive. It has assimilated those forces, it has given them a rhythm which now inspires its art, spirituality and its whole life. And it is thus contributing to the greatness of our common civilization.
So, no wonder that in many of those African states external policies are mainly based on the problems of concern to Africa in general. The greater number of new African states are first of all concerned with their own problems. As exceptions to that rule we might mention Mali and Guinea, which are taking an active part in the discussion of more general matters of international interest.
African states frequently meet to adopt certain stands. In fact, they met recently at Monrovia and at Casablanca, where African chiefs took the opportunity to strengthen the friendly relations that must exist between their countries, as well as to determine the policy to be adopted in the United Nations in regard to colonialism, the Congo, Algeria and all the other matters of concern to their continent.
African states of French language already exert a moderating influence within the Afro-Asiatic bloc in the United Nations. They are not in general interested in taking side in the cold war or in following the Afro-Asiatic group when the latter decides to launch an open attack against countries still practising colonialism. However, they have already supported moderate resolutions to put an end to colonialism. Above all they especially strive, and I repeat "especially", to establish friendly relations with the Canadian delegation and With other bi-cultural countries.
In concluding my remarks on this particular subject, I wish to indicate briefly the decisions taken by those new African countries:
1.	They gave vigorous support to the admission of Mauritania to the United Nations.
2.	They acted as mediators between France and Algerian nationalists.
3.	French-speaking African states opposed the apartheid policy of the government of the Union of South Africa.
90205-6-513
Supply-External Affairs
4.	Concerning the Congo, they supported the recognition of the Kasavubu delegation before the general assembly.
Finally, it is to be noted that they played an active part in the deliberations of certain commissions. For example, I emphasize that my friend Mr. Ernest Gassou of Haute-Volta has been appointed commissioner to supervise the legislative elections in Ruanda-Urundi and that Guinea, Senegal and Mali are all members of the United Nations control commission in the Congo.
The fifteenth session of the United Nations has been called the African session. That is why the discussion of the problems of territories under trusteeship and under mandate were the object of very special attention on the part of the fourth commission.
I had the honour of representing Canada on that commission and I should like to report briefly on the most important discussions that took place there.
The most important resolution supported by Canada concerning the territories under trusteeship was a pressing appeal to the administering powers urging them to give administrative experience to the natives in all sectors of public administration, avoiding every discrimination, so that those territories would have an administration already set up when they reach independence. That resolution was heartily welcomed by the African states and only a few nations still steeped in colonialism opposed it.
A problem which, I think, was very difficult to work out was the future of Ruanda-Urundi, a country under Belgian trusteeship. Let me outline the situation, so that it will be better understood.
Serious disturbances broke out in Ruanda in the fall of 1959. Their cause was the strife for the provisional leadership of the country between the tribes, one called Tutsi, a class of feudal tradition, and the other called Hutu, which had always been the servants of the Tutsi and representing 85 per cent of the population. The Muami, an African term applied to the king of Ruanda, who had left the territory a few months before, identified himself with the Tutsi tribe and his return is, of course, opposed by the tribes who wish to retain power.
Having heard the testimony of the political parties, the fourth commission advised both parties to work together towards the national reconciliation of the country, in order to give it an adequate preparation to independence anticipated for 1961.
After a long discussion, the commission passed two resolutions on Ruanda-Urundi. The purpose of the first resolution was to invite Belgium, the administrative authority,

Supply-External Affairs to grant an unconditional amnesty to all political convicts, in order to bring about a climate of understanding and of reconciliation.
Moreover, the resolution advocated that a round table conference be held by all the political parties of the country, United Nations observers being present, and that afterwards the United Nations supervise the legislative election for the independence of the territory which was anticipated for 1961 as I have mentioned a moment ago.
The second resolution recommended the return of Muami to Ruanda and, for that purpose, the institution of a referendum in order to seek out the opinion of the people on that matter.
When I went to that country, my task was to supervise the amnesty called for by the first resolution, and I must say that the judicial commission of the United Nations has enjoyed, during its work, the closest co-operation on the part of Belgian authorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house took recess this morning, I was explaining the purpose of the judiciary mission sent to Ruanda-Urundi by the United Nations. I was saying that when a United Nations resolution was submitted, the administrative authorities were ordered to grant unconditional amnesty to the political prisoners of 1959 in the territory of Ruanda-Urundi. Our commission was entrusted especially with the revision of the rulings of the special courts established on that occasion by the administrative authorities. At the conclusion of my remarks this morning, I stated that in accordance with the United Nations resolution, we succeeded in releasing practically all political prisoners who had been jailed following the 1959 uprising. However, I must admit that the release of those political leaders had a disastrous effect, since it gave rise to new disturbances between the tribes. At the present time hundreds of people are killed in that territory every week.
I fear that Ruanda-Urundi will one day be the scene of bloodshed. I do not wish to imply

that Belgium is fully responsible for those troubles, but I feel that the United Nations should in the future take a closer look at the social and political conditions prevailing in those emergent countries before giving them their political independence and sovereignty.
Another matter which engaged the attention of the fourth commission concerned the holding of a plebiscite in the south and the north of the Cameroon.
The result of that plebiscite conducted by a United Nations representative showed that the north of the Cameroon wanted to join with Nigeria while the south of the Cameroon wished to unite with the Cameroon Republic, recently created.
The validity of the plebiscite was questioned by the Cameroon Republic on the grounds of fraud and discrimination in the running of the referendum by the United Nations representative and by Great Britain which was the administering authority of the territory. The Cameroon Republic was asking in particular that a committee of the United Nations be set up to investigate the irregularities of that referendum before North Cameroon could be permitted to join with Nigeria. That debate, in my opinion, was one of the most stormy of the fourth commission. Events reached such a climax that during the debate, the delegates of the Cameroon Republic left the meeting with a large number of African representatives and France accused the chairman of showing bias in conducting the proceedings.
On that occasion, the Canadian representative made a very moderate speech, while strongly supporting the report of the United Nations commissioner concerning the holding of the referendum. Canada however refused to support Great Britain's resolution because that would have seriously impaired our prestige with the African countries.
The general assembly adopted the resolution acknowledging the validity of the United Nations referendum by a two thirds majority.
Those are the most important events which marked the fourth commission and especially the second part of the fifteenth session.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to emphasize the devotion and work of the hon. members- government members as well as opposition members and the third party members-who came to New York. I wish to commend the devotion of the government officials who attended that meeting.
The prestige of our country at the United Nations is excellent. For that we are grateful to the parliamentary secretary to the minister (Mr. Nesbitt) and more particularly to the

Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) who has a way of asserting himself by his frankness, his loyalty and his tenacity in the discussion of international problems.
The Canadian resolution on disarmament was supported by many delegations, 18 to be exact, because the minister was able to prove to other nations that disarmament is not the business of great powers alone, but that all countries who wish the well-being of humankind must tackle that question to find a quick solution.
In the international sphere, Canada has become an emancipated power which must not be content to act as a negotiating agent between countries, but must stay in the forefront in order to find solutions to world problems.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, Canada is now exerting a beneficial influence in the international community, because all nations understand that we have no colonial past nor any territorial ambitions, but that our sole desire is to save from definite peril the principles of freedom and real democracy, in trying to develop among all peoples of the world the cult of spiritual values, which alone can give this very disturbed world the guarantee of a lasting peace.
