speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday, in what I thought was a very impressive contribution to this discussion, my colleague the hon. member for Essex East reminded us that it was 22 years ago on that very day that this House of Commons was called into session to ratify and confirm a declaration of war against, not the German people, but against Nazi tyranny and Nazi aggression. In his very thoughtful and realistic examination of the situation today the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed this committee, and I quote his words, that "the world is hovering on the brink of war". These words were repeated by a man who will have far more to do with the waging of war, if not with the making of the peace, than the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Today that man, Mr. Khrushchev, according to press reports, in Moscow when he said "mankind is on the brink of another military tragedy" which is his way of saying the same thing. We are on the brink of a war which we have been saying to ourselves for years in unthinkable. Everybody is thinking about it now.
In August, 1914, in the realm of opinion and of emotion, war was not unthinkable. Indeed, at that time-and many of us will remember our reaction to the developing circumstances of that month which seems so long ago now-war exercised almost a horrible fascination for many people who knew 90205-6-5134
Supply-External Affairs nothing about it except in terms of the charge of the light brigade or the thin red line. It was that reaction which endangered peace in 1914 and made war perhaps inevitable at that time. There was just enough of that feeling 22 years ago, that war was not unthinkable, to ensure that it happened. If we had felt in the 1930's that war was not only thinkable but likely in view of the policy of Hitler and his Nazi gang, if we had felt that it was thinkable and probable we might not have had it; we might have stopped it. If we had stopped it then we might not be talking about it today.
I think, Mr. Chairman, one danger which we face in the world today is the very opposite to our popular reaction far back in 1914, because we know now that war is so horrible that it literally is unthinkable with the 100 megaton continental destroyer bomb which Khrushchev boasts he can make; and perhaps he can, and also the Americans. If it is so ghastly, then let us not think about it. This is the kind of reaction you get in some quarters in the summer of 1961, the kind of reaction which is reflected on a United States magazine cover which I looked at the other day on which in very black type were the words "Pigskin Preview" and underneath, in smaller type, "Berlin Crisis".
The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated yesterday, and quite rightly, that the situation is tense and serious. There was in his speech-and I am certainly not criticizing him for this-none of the optimism, dogged and determined optimism, that he has shown in the past. At times he has chided us a little for being too pessimistic, and I am certainly not chiding him for being too optimistic in those days because optimism with endeavour is a good foundation for international activity. Now we are facing a serious and tense situation. He said quite rightly that we should face it in this country and in other countries with cool consideration, neither with despair which would be wrong, nor with panic, which might be fatal. In this situation all of us in this house would wish to approach this subject and subjects related to it on a plane far above that of partisan politics or parliamentary tactics, because it is this kind of situation which emphasizes that there are so many stronger things that unite us than divide us. National unity is essential and I believe is possible in times of national or international crisis.
At the moment the centre of our fears is the city of Berlin, but there are other areas of tension in the world, and our fears in the past ten years have switched from one area of tension to another. While we are concentrating on Berlin and all that it stands for at the moment we also have to worry about-I am

Supply-External Affairs sure the government is not unaware of this, especially the Secretary of State for External Affairs-Southeast Asia, Laos, North Africa, Algeria, Tunis and Cuba on our own hemisphere and Tibet in Asia. All these tensions in a sense are related to each other, and the drama and the tragedy of the crisis shift from one to another. Now it is Berlin which is the centre of the current crisis of a recurrent cold war.
All of us have been listening to a great deal of talk about this current crisis. Over the air, in the newspapers, from official reports and official statements we get an analysis of what is wrong and what is right and what is going on, and we get analyses of the analysis; we get interpretation, and we get interpretations of the interpretation. I think perhaps all of us get sometimes a little foggy and confused as to what is happening and what can be done to prevent its deteriorating into war. All this talk, in my view, especially the words which emanate from communist centres, is too often what Father Pire, the distinguished Belgian priest, and the recipient of a Nobel Peace Prize, once called the dialogue of the deaf. At times the words used do not mean anything, often not even to the people who utter them, certainly not to us who have to listen to them because many words now have no value. That coinage has been debased when words like peace, democracy and non-aggression can be used in the language of communism to mean something exactly the opposite to that which has always been their natural meaning and significance. Mr. Khrushchev, in a message to the French government on September 5, just two or three days ago, is quoted in the press as saying this:
The people of West Berlin must themselves determine the social-economic system of their city and enter into free relations with any state.
That sentiment, Mr. Chairman, is irreproachable. It is equally irreproachable when it is applied, as it should be applied, not only to Berlin but to East Germany and to all other peoples under foreign domination. Yet, if these words represent the policy of Khrushchev's government and his own personal attitude, we ask ourselves, where is the crisis in West Berlin? He says that the people of West Berlin must themselves determine the social-economic system of their city and enter into free relations with any state, or presumably group of states. So what is the crisis about?
The crisis is not resolved by words like this because we in the west do not take such words at their face value, so deep is our distrust and our fear, with good evidence on which to base that distrust and fear, and because words like that have been contradicted by the same man in other speeches not very long before the one I have just

mentioned. It was Mr. Khrushchev, was it not, or some representative of Mr. Khrushchev-I am not sure which-who said not long ago that the Soviet government would not be the first to resume nuclear tests.
I think Mr. Khrushchev said that again recently in an interview with Mr. Sulzberger of the New York Times.
How can you reconcile that kind of contradiction and how do you get any comfort out of such reassuring statements as the one I have mentioned, especially in the face of some less reassuring ones that appear in the papers today? This is another indication of the gulf that divides us. Perhaps Mr. Khrushchev himself would say, "Oh, well, we are not the first to resume tests", because France, one of the founding and important members of NATO, itself started nuclear tests after he, Mr. Khrushchev, had made his earlier renunciation of tests.
It is because of this feeling that the principles which Mr. Khrushchev has embodied in these words, applied to the situation in West Berlin, and meant no doubt to be reassuring to us, are not reassuring. We must get some concrete assurance in a form that is more effective than words that the principles themselves will be observed. To put it brutally and frankly, we have no faith or little faith in what he says, especially when it is contradicted by what he has said previously and by what he is doing while he speaks.
So we look for some other assurance that will embody and protect these principles, and in the case of Berlin we have had one now for a good many years, as all members know, in the four-power agreement of 1945. The situation which is accepted in that agreement covering Berlin and also a divided Germany, is an anomalous one as we look at it now. It seems to me, with that hindsight which makes everything so much easier, that it was a very foolish agreement indeed to have entered into. But it was a very formal one. The conditions that existed at the time it was entered into, and this may help us to understand why it was done, were very different from what they are now. At the present time, it is unnecessary to underline the fact, there is no good will, no co-operation, no desire to implement this agreement any longer on the Soviet side nor has there been for some time past. In fact, the Russians have made it quite clear to the world that they are determined to alter the present situation in Berlin, to alter that earlier agreement by which the west Berliners were guaranteed freedom and the western allies were guaranteed rights.

Mr. Khrushchev made this perfectly clear at the end of 1958, I believe it was, when he said frankly what he was going to do and he even set a time limit within which he would do it. Our position on the western side, a position that I think has been rightly taken by the governments concerned, is that we cannot admit that agreements of this kind can be abrogated by force or the threat of force. It would be, of course, the very negation of international diplomacy. It would make good international relations impossible. It would create an impossible situation if the west yielded to this kind of atomic blackmail, as it has been called. It would set up a kind of chain reaction. We would go from pressure to pressure and yielding to yielding until we would not know where it would ends. As the French proverb says: "l'appetit vient en mangeant".
Surely we have learned since 1914, Mr. Chairman, that peace is not ensured by surrender to blackmail. Indeed, war is sometimes made inevitable by such surrender. So we ask ourselves: Is there no choice then between the impossible alternatives of suicide or surrender? There must be. But I do not think we will save ourselves from this situation and others like it by merely relying on armed force to avoid a choice.
We have to be armed in the west. Unilateral disarmament would be an invitation to catastrophe, but armaments themselves will not do the job. The dilemma with which we are faced, this awful choice, which some people through oversimplification of the problem, try to force on us, of suicide by atomic war or surrender by yielding to atomic threats; this necessity, as some see it, of relying primarily, if not exclusively, on arms to avoid a choice; this dilemma and the impossibility of resolving it by arms alone, have been very well put by professor Hugh Seaton Watson in what I thought was a very wise book entitled "Neither War Nor Peace". I quote a paragraph from that book, where he said:
One may agree that it would indeed be better to accept communist domination or any other form of totalitarian tyranny in the hope that with the passage of time later generations may restore liberty rather than see the whole human race destroyed, but this is not in fact the alternative that faces the governments of the west.
Or, I might interpolate, the peoples of the west. He goes on:
The choice is not between the certainty of destruction of the human race and the certainty of communist domination but between the possibility of destruction if the west retains atomic weapons and the certainty of Soviet domination at least of Europe if the west unilaterally renounces atomic weapons.
Then he adds this sentence with which I think all of us will agree:
Supply-External Affairs
If the alternative is put in this form most noncommunist Europeans and Americans would prefer the risk to the certainty.
We have heard it said more than once in this debate, Mr. Chairman, that there are people in Canada who say-I know I have talked to some of them who have spoken along these lines and there have been letters in the press expressing the same view-"we will not fight for Berlin or for Germany". To use the words used by the hon. member for Kootenay West in his speech, that would be a monstrous absurdity. I think he put it that way, and it would be a monstrous absurdity in one sense. Many of us have no cause to love those elements in German society which were responsible for the war of 1914 and the war of 1939. It seems to be almost unnatural to line ourselves up alongside those people some of whom-but only some-were responsible for what happened from 1933 to 1945. But Mr. Chairman, surely this is the wrong approach to the problem and represents a misunderstanding of the position. We would not in any event be fighting for Berlin any more than we fought for Korea or for Danzig. We would only, if we were obliged to do so, be resisting aggression, fighting for a principle or fighting for a freedom which is not limited to any one small area of the world.
If we put the problem in those other terms, that we would be fighting for the Germans, we will get into nothing but misunderstanding and trouble. As a matter of fact, if after 1919 we had shown more understanding of those forces in Germany which were just as much opposed as we were to Kaiserism and all it stood for, and if after 1919 we had given the Social Democratic regime in Germany more support and more understanding, we might not have had to fight Nazi aggression and Nazi tyranny in 1939. Therefore, we surely do not want to do anything, by ill considered observations about Germany and about Berlin either, which would discourage those in Germany who are now governing a democratic republic.
As I have said then, the alternative in certain contingencies to resistance against aggression, if that were forced-and it is the only kind of resistance we would be taking part in-would be to surrender to force or the threat of force backed up by nuclear blackmail exploiting our fears. In that case we would have become the captive of our fears by giving in; just as we would become the victim of our fears if we took panic action. I suggest then, Mr. Chairman-and I do not think there will be any disagreement with this statement-that we in the west cannot yield to force or blackmail. As it is so often

Supply-External Affairs put, we must stand firm. But as Walter Lipp-mann mentioned in his column this morning and it has been said by others previously, standing firm is not the same as standing pat. We must realize-and I believe the government does so-that the present situation in Berlin and in Germany created at a time when circumstances were far different than they are today, is not going to last indefinitely and that change will come. In the period between the two wars we used to talk a great deal about the necessity for peaceful change; and it was resistance to peaceful change from 1919 to 1939 that had something to do with the catastrophe of 1939. So change will come. But it must be change not brought about by force and not brought about by betrayal, which I think is a far better way of putting it than by saying we must not give in to appeasement. Force today in terms of armed action, which would mean nuclear war, cannot reunite a divided country any more than force of that kind today can liberate people from the ruins which that kind of liberation would bring about. Surely there must be another and a better way. This necessity for eventual and peaceful change-and I return to it-surely is shown by the very nature of the earlier agreements that were made. At the time they were made those agreements were not intended to be permanent even by those who made them inasmuch as they visualized the eventual reunification of Germany through co-operation between the occupying powers and Berlin as the capital of a united Germany. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we must be realistic about this situation. I think the German feeling for unity must be respected, of course. However, that does not mean that we should give any encouragement to any German feeling for reunification by force or action which would risk imminent war for such unification. Nor does it mean that we should ignore or encourage our German friends and allies to ignore the problems of the eastern boundary, the Oder-Neisse line or the problem of Polish and Russian fears and susceptibilities which are very real and genuine. These susceptibilities are understandable in the light of the human and material destruction these people have suffered in wars from German invaders. I think also, in order to be realistic, we must realize that a Russian rejection-because that is what it is-of a non-communist united Germany, which to them would be anticommunist, in association with NATO and the west, is strong and it is opposed by equally strong western insistence on the right of Germany to remain in NATO for defence and indeed for European development; and we are not likely to weaken on that score. That is a dilemma and I cannot now see any way out of 

it. We are going to have to live with it as we shall have to live with many unpleasant things for some time. However, the problem now is to prevent this dilemma from deteriorating into a crisis and the use of force. All this means that Berlin as a problem cannot be isolated from the German problem and from the whole problem of relationships inside the cold war.
When we talk about the necessity of negotiating these matters, we know that it will take a long time. I do not think we in the west should refuse, for instance, to consider the possibility, as part of a general settlement, of disengagement or pulling back of the forces from the east and from the west. I think that this is a negotiable matter. Very respectable western leaders have put that suggestion forward in the past, including Sir Anthony Eden. It is negotiable but it is certainly not negotiable on Soviet terms as we now know them and it is not negotiable either at the expense of the freedom of any section of the German people. I do not know whether or not the whole position of our collective security arrangements in Europe are negotiable because I do not have all the facts in order to enable me to come to a judgment on that matter. However, I know or at least I am sure in my own mind that the proposals put forward in the New Democratic party resolutions dealing with this particular matter are not those to which I could subscribe. I read one sentence from these proposals:
To relieve tensions Canada should press for a demilitarized zone in central Europe.
I think that is arguable and certainly should be looked into. But then it goes on to say this:
To relieve tensions Canada should press for the simultaneous disbandment of the Warsaw and the NATO pacts.
That puts these two collective security arrangements on exactly the same basis. It assumes that if NATO and the Warsaw pacts were abrogated the results would be equal, in terms of security. We know, surely, that this is not the case and disbandment of NATO would be the abandonment of free peoples. The break up of NATO would mean that its democratic members would be split apart and collective action would go.
What would the break up of the Warsaw pact mean? Perhaps nothing at all. Perhaps it would be almost as simple without the pact as with it for the Soviet government to control and determine the action of the armies of the present members of the Warsaw pact. Therefore to have these two organizations on the same level of importance so far as international security is concerned, and to suggest that their simultaneous disbandment would

not prejudice the situation in any way to our disadvantage seems to me to be entirely unrealistic and indeed dangerous.
If the existing guarantee of Berlin, which goes back to 1944, is a shaky one in present circumstances, I suspect it will become even shakier when the responsibility on the communist side for carrying it out is transferred, as it is going to be transferred, to an East German communist government as a result of a peace treaty made with that government by the Soviet union. Because after that time so far as the Russians are concerned it will be the responsibility of the East German satellite under Soviet domination to observe the stipulations of that agreement.
This would mean a transfer of authority and a recognition of East Germany as an independent, sovereign state by a great many nations, particularly the communist states in the world. A great many of them have already given this recognition. This would perhaps mean a deterioration of the situation. It might mean additional dangers, but I cannot myself think this is a matter over which there need be war.
The Prime Minister in his speech at Winnipeg, to which I have already referred, asked a rhetorical question in that connection. I think it was a good one. I cannot quote his exact words but it was to the effect: "People say, is the recognition of the east German government, is that alone the kind of thing that should result in a crisis which would involve war?" I do not think so. After all, we recognize in fact, if not in law, what the Minister of Agriculture calls the Chinese democratic republic and we do business with it. Perhaps we will find ourselves doing business shortly with the "East German democratic republic". I would hate to see the western powers adopt an intransigent position on that particular point. But they have the right, of course, to do what can be done and must be done to insist that this transfer and this recognition shall not affect the rights and freedoms of the people of West Berlin or the rights of access to West Berlin by those who now have them.
Under this change, so we are told, the allied forces would still have the right to be in Berlin and the right to get to Berlin. Their presence there is still the symbol of the freedom of the people and the symbol of western rights. I think it would have to be preserved. And we now have in Berlin an increase in western military strength following the deterioration of the position there after the closing of the boundary and as a prelude to the transfer of all authority to the East German communist republic through a peace treaty with that government.

We now have additional western soldiers there. We have those soldiers armed and equipped and facing East German soldiers who are armed and equipped. We learn from the newspapers and from the picture magazines that they are only a few feet apart. They are pointing guns at each other. The other day there was a water cannon fired and there was a reply by a tear gas bomb. One cannot help having nightmares over the possibility of something else being exchanged across that tense and nervous border. Unless there is some way in which that situation can be stabilized these people will continue facing each other at 10 paces, which is usually the prelude to a duel.
What can be done about this? If the guarantee we have, and which we are entitled in the west to insist upon because of the freedoms that it gives the people of West Berlin, is shaky, and if it is getting shakier, and if it is creating these tensions which might explode any minute, is there anything we can do by negotiation to stabilize the position without giving away any essential rights?
I come back to the proposition which I have made and which others have made in the last few weeks, and indeed the last few months. I remember talking about this when Mr. Khrushchev said sometime ago that he was going to have a peace treaty on a certain date with East Germany and after that there would be trouble if there was not some change made on the western side.
An alternative form of guarantee which I think is negotiable and one which I think has the best chance of working out-although I do not underestimate the difficulties *-would be the United Nations replacing the existing agreement with a formal international guarantee; with a United Nations police force inside Berlin and United Nations police forces on the access routes to Berlin to secure that guarantee.
I know the United Nations has had a pretty rough time lately and some of the hopes, and indeed some of the faith people had in the ability of this world organization to help guarantee international peace and security and to provide the kind of international force behind international law which would strengthen peace and security have disappeared in the unhappy developments of the last year or so.
I know the Soviet union-the minister spoke about this yesterday, and other hon. members have spoken about it-has given at least an indication in its attitude at the United Nations that it is not now too concerned whether or not the organization survives. Perhaps I had better put it in this way, that it is more and more insistent that if

Supply-External Affairs it is to survive it will be in a form that will be acceptable to the communist world. That means in a form that ensures there will be a communist veto over every activity of the organization from the secretary general down. I refer to the now famous troika theory of international organization. But this danger to the United Nations does not surely alter the fact that we should work even harder to strengthen it. This is an opportunity to that end.
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs who has already given a strong indication of his loyalty to this organization, will desire to make it stronger in the interests of peace. I am sure he will do what he can to strengthen it in this connection.
Somehow, perhaps through the "mobilization of the middle", the United Nations must be brought in to guarantee the freedom of West Berlin within the context of Mr. Khrushchev's own statement, about which he should continually be reminded. The United Nations could also guarantee the rights of access of the western powers to Berlin.
This could be done through a United Nations police force. Perhaps it would be possible to transfer some of the United Nations police force from Palestine until we had a separate group for this particular purpose. Perhaps it would also be possible to strengthen the presence of the United Nations in Berlin, by moving some of its activities into that city. I read this morning a letter in the Montreal Gazette which mentioned the idea of moving into Berlin of some of the European activities of the United Nations. United Nations agencies could be moved into Berlin and it could become a centre of international activity. Geneva is already becoming crowded, so some of the European activities and agencies of the United Nations and those concerning the Middle East, could be transferred into Berlin. It should become a permanent centre of United Nations activity. This might create a situation in Berlin over which it would be more difficult for communist powers to ride roughshod than if we have two or three thousand allied troops behind a wall there.
I would hope that this idea could be pursued at the forthcoming general assembly. The important thing, surely, is to remember that the present situation itself is not permanent in Berlin or in a disunited Germany, but also to remember that any changing of that situation by force will provoke resistance which might mean war. There should be no doubt in anybody's mind on either side that this might happen. Then, we would have to start finding another way, making a change at this time, which 10 or 15 years

from now would become inevitable in any event. We must use the United Nations for this purpose.
Now, I admit that all this has been made more difficult by the recent announcement of the resumption of nuclear tests. Every member of the house who has spoken in this debate, Mr. Chairman, has mentioned this unhappy development which represented, I think it is fair to say, a cynical betrayal by the Soviet union of the hopes which up until a few months ago at least we had placed in the possibility of a united front in this one aspect of disarmament. This is a phase of disarmament to which the Soviet union itself, in years gone by, attached the greatest importance. But now, and I do not think I am putting it too strongly, they have used it for blackmail by terror.
I do not know-I ask-whether any protest has been made by the Canadian government to the Soviet union, except in public statements, over this resumption of nuclear tests and the torpedoing of the Geneva conference at a time when the positions, on paper at least, were coming closer together.
If I have any criticism of the technique of disarmament negotiation as exemplified by this Geneva conference, and it applies to other disarmament meetings going back 10 or 12 years now, it is that we in the west allow ourselves slowly and gradually to be pushed into positions we would not accept at the beginning. By the time we get to a position of acceptance, then something else happens and the Soviet union refuses to accept the new position. A very good example of this is what has been happening in Geneva in the last few months. The last offer which was made, if it had been made a year ago, would have been an infinitely more difficult one for the Russians to refuse than when it was made a few weeks ago. This is an unhappy development, then, which is making negotiation more difficult. But it makes such negotiation more essential than ever before.
There is another aspect of this problem which has been mentioned by more than one speaker, and it is a growingly important aspect. I refer to the influence that can be brought to bear on this whole issue by what are now known as the uncommitted countries. I was at an unofficial, private conference in Oxford a few days ago at which there were many delegates from the uncommitted countries. But, they never talked of themselves as being uncommitted but as being representatives of the third world. What can this third world do to redress the balance between the powers of the west and the east? The Belgrade conference was an interesting indication of the possibilities and limitations of this new force in the world.

It is true that the resumption of tests by the Russians did, in a sense, if I may use a colloquialism, take the heat off the attack on colonialism which otherwise would have dominated the discussions at Belgrade. It is true also that this conference in Belgrade did take some action, as a third force, in trying to get the situation solved, as they saw the situation, in Moscow and in Washington. If such a result was achieved in Belgrade, I think we owe a great deal to Mr. Nehru, as one additional contribution he has made to peace. In all the talk about colonialism, neocolonialism and the iniquities of western imperialism that came out of that conference, Mr. Nehru had as much reason from past history to join in that talk as anybody else, but it was his cool, calm voice which pointed out that the danger now is not colonialism, it is destruction. I think he got that conference to take a line which it would not have otherwise followed if he had not been there. Perhaps this great man, one of the great men in our contemporary world, could be persuaded to take a lead at the forthcoming meetings of the United Nations to mobilize this feeling in the middle powers that humanity is not going to be permitted to be destroyed by the great powers. I understand he is going to Washington soon, and I hope he will also be coming to Ottawa on this visit.
There is one factor in this mobilization of the uncommitted nations which we cannot ignore. That is their underlying suspicion of what they still call colonial imperialism and neo-colonialism. I learned last week as I have learned on so many occasions in the past, that to many of these countries who have recently gained independence, colonialism is thought of in terms of conquest and occupation from across the sea, of racialism and discrimination. But this kind of colonialism, what is known as salt water colonialism, is on the way out. The pro-consuls have departed or they are going. There is no danger to free peoples from them now except in one or two areas of the world which are a little behind the times. The balance of good and evil that came from occupation by imperial powers across the water, can be left to history to decide. Perhaps it should be forgotten today in the face of this greater and immediate danger.
Furthermore these new peoples should realize that while that old type of colonialism is on the way out, there is a far more dangerous form of colonialism which is, up to the present, still on the way in. I refer to the colonialism not of imperial forces going across an ocean but in legions moving across a border in the service of communist imperialism and destroying old nations and old civilizations. The nature of this new imperialism was made quite clear by Mr. Khrushchev at the
Supply-External Affairs communist congress at the beginning of this year when he said, and communist doctrine is now officially established along this line, that it is the right and duty of communist powers, communist parties and communist peoples throughout the world to assist others in the struggle for liberation. This is his way of referring to these wars of which the communists approve. It is that spurious doctrine that has caused Russians and Chinese to cross borders and destroy ancient and civilized societies.
I know that at the forthcoming meeting of the United Nations assembly we will be facing, as we have been facing in the past, resolutions condemning colonialism. The Prime Minister made a strong speech last year on this subject. After these speeches have been made and when the resolutions are being discussed in committee, that is the time to try to alter these resolutions to make them convey the right meaning of colonialism. We must insist on that kind of discussion, making sure all nations are made aware, as we are aware, of what the new colonialism means.
Before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about NATO because the minister and others have said a great deal about it. I should like to refer to the influence of NATO on these developments, what NATO can do and what NATO is not doing. I recall that a year ago in this house I talked about NATO and made a plea for a stronger NATO. I was rather gloomy about some of the prospects for NATO, and I talked about it being at the crossroads. I was chided by the Secretary of State for External Affairs for being so pessimistic. Everything I have read about NATO in the last year has confirmed me in my anxiety. If the members of NATO do not get closer together, they are going to get farther apart. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that this is a defensive alliance. Of course, it is a defensive alliance to us but it is not to those who are opposing us-at least, so they say. We are told that NATO must be kept strong, and that is true. However, in this difficult situation strength is more than military strength. It is also unity.
But what worries me about NATO, and I have no doubt it worries the Secretary of State for External Affairs too, is the disunity that appears now in the co-ordination of foreign policy among NATO members.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that there cannot be any smaller directorate inside NATO to tell the other NATO members what they should or should not do. I agree there must be equality inside NATO in that area even though there cannot be equality of power or responsibility. But if

Supply-External Affairs there is to be that kind of equality there should be a much greater effort made than has been made in the last ten or 15 years in NATO to co-ordinate and unify the foreign policies of the members of NATO before a crisis develops.
A spokesman of the government, I think the Prime Minister, said after the meeting of the foreign ministers of the three main western powers in Paris last August, that this showed how great the unity of NATO was in the face of threats from the Soviet union. Unity in the face of threats is always an immediate result in our coalition. But that meeting also showed, if the reports I read were at all accurate, that while there was this kind of unity against aggression there was also disunity on how that threat of aggression should be met. I think we must somehow do more than we have in the past to unify foreign policy of the NATO members or we will not be able to co-ordinate defence policy and stand united against aggression.
In this connection I wish to repeat what my friend the hon. member for Essex East said about a sentence in the resolution of the New Democratic party with respect to NATO and foreign policy. That sentence has been placed on the record before, but I wish to repeat it:
The New party believes that we should seek a reappraisal and change of NATO's policies and objectives.
I have no quarrel with that. We should always be reappraising and re-examining NATO's policies and objectives and I have made that statement myself more than once. The resolution goes on to state:
The New party believes that the extension of nuclear weapons to any further states and alliances threatens disaster to the world. It therefore opposes Canada's troops being supplied with such weapons at home or abroad. At present, except for those nations which have independently developed atomic capacity, neither NATO itself nor its members individually possess or control nuclear warheads.
I think that is true, except for the United States, the United Kingdom and France. The following is the part of the resolution with which I do not agree. It reads:
Should they do so, Canada must make it clear that it cannot remain in the alliance.
In other words, should any of the other members of NATO accept nuclear warheads either nationally or presumably under NATO control, Canada must make it clear that Canada cannot remain in the alliance. For instance, if the Netherlands inside NATO accepted nuclear warheads under Netherlands control or presumably under NATO control, Canada should withdraw from the alliance. I wish to make it perfectly clear that our party does not subscribe to any doctrine of that nature. We do agree, however, that there must be made a much greater effort inside NATO

in the field of co-ordination of foreign policy and planning in the future than there has been in the past; that collective policies in NATO must be worked out in advance to the greatest possible extent rather than left at times to the impulsive reaction of individual members. There is a weakness here which should be corrected in the planning inside the alliance.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the blocking off of East Berlin by the east German government was foreseen by the governments represented in the NATO council. It must have been obvious that this was going to happen before long. The communist leaders told us it was going to happen. If that is the case, were plans made inside NATO to meet that particular emergency when it occurred? Mr. Khrushchev told us about it in 1958, but when it happened one received the impression that it took the western alliance by surprise. In saying that I appreciate that I do not have all of the knowledge and facts and therefore I do not speak dogmatically on these matters.
We know at this moment that the attempted blocking off of access to Berlin may occur, the attempt is likely to be made; I put it no higher than that. Have we in the NATO alliance agreed plans to meet that blockade or will we react impulsively after the emergency situation develops? You can put this particular exigency in frightening concrete terms if you so desire. What do we do now in the western alliance if a convoy is stopped by the east German forces on the access road to Berlin or if a plane is forced down in the corridor to Berlin? If that should happen, has NATO an agreed policy as to what should be done? Have they made clear to the other side what is likely to happen if it is tried? If we are going to resist this sort of thing because it is aggression by force, have we enough force in NATO in Europe to ensure that it can be made effective without-and this is the terrifying prospect-falling back on nuclear retaliation. Surely that is the most critical question that faces the world at the present time and it is focused right on this particular situation in terms of this particular possibility.
Of course, I am not asking the government to tell the committee what action the NATO governments are proposing to take in a situation of this kind. I am asking whether the NATO governments are looking ahead and planning to take united action in such an emergency so there will be no temptation on the part of any single government in NATO to take impulsive action under pressures which perhaps may not be wise.
As I have said outside the house I am without knowledge of all the facts and am

therefore not being too critical of this, but I think the United States reaction the other day in resuming nuclear tests was obviously taken under great pressure-congressional or pentagon, or both, I do not know-but it was taken at a time when, if it could have been put off for a few days or weeks, the United States might have made a great impact on the political cold war at the forthcoming United Nations assembly. Because that action was taken under pressure perhaps some of that advantage has been thrown away. I hope, therefore, if we have to face these emergency situations in the future-and I have just mentioned two of them-we will be considering and planning in advance what course we will take and it will not be left to any power to act quickly and perhaps, because we are all human, impulsively, when the emergency takes place.
What is required as the minister pointed out so well yesterday is wisdom and calm resolution as we face these awful situations. What is required is a policy planned and agreed in advance. What is required is the avoidance of sudden policies which, if you like, throw us out into outer space without having made any provision for diplomatic re-entry. What is required is the avoidance of impulsive, panicky, sudden reactions. What is required is a policy which weighs all the risks and opportunities; which establishes the price to pay for peace without the loss of freedom; which realizes what nuclear war means but also makes clear the risk of surrender to the threat of it. As someone said yesterday speaking in the debate, we will not be respected by being weak. That is true, but we will not be respected either by being panicky or rash as was also said yesterday.
As the minister pointed out, a great deal of sacrifice and effort will be required over a long time, sacrifice and effort as never before. As the Pope reminded us yesterday in a statement from Rome, peace is not a luxury. Creative peace has to be bought and paid for by those who wish to enjoy it. That kind of peace is worth a very high price. Perhaps I may be pardoned for quoting what I said on this very point as far back as 1951. I said this:
That kind of peace is worth paying for. The military dangers which threaten the free world at many points are so grave that we will all have to pay a substantial price to protect the peace we value.
This was ten years ago. 1 continue:
We will have to rearm in co-operation with our allies. We will have to pay for rearmament through heavier taxation. We will have to work harder. We will have to forgo some of the luxuries to which we had looked forward. I am sure that Canadians will not complain of these sacrifices when they remember the cause in which they are made.
I went on:

But there is one price which we will not pay even to secure peace. There are some things we value even more than peace. We will not pay for it by sacrificing our own freedom or the freedom of other countries.
I do not believe that we will have to pay that price. I cannot believe it. Have the resources of man, man's mind, man's heart, man's soul, sunk so low that we will have to pay that price for the avoidance of planetary destruction?
President de Gaulle said on September 5 -and I must say I did not think too highly of those particular words:
War whatever it might bring to the west, would certainly result in the complete overturning of the Soviet regime.
It will do that, but it will result in far more than that, the destruction of vast areas and peoples of this planet, the overturning of much more than the Soviet regime. A nuclear holocaust over Berlin at this time-and we are talking about that; we are told we are on the brink of it-would be grotesque in its absurdity; it would be complete in its consequences and it would be all embracing in its destruction. This must not happen. And so I say, Mr. Chairman-and as I conclude I come back to where I was a few moments ago -let world opinion, expressed through the United Nations, on the eve of this assembly, declare that it will not happen and take action to prevent it by the mobilization of world opinion in the assembly of the world. Canada can play and has played a good part in this kind of mobilization. I am sure that Canada will play a good and strong part at the forthcoming assembly in the mobilization of opinion to reject extermination. Therefore, let us return then to the United Nations in this crisis and let us return to the force which, with all its weaknesses, it can exert. I have never seen this put in better words than these, and as I conclude I may be permitted to read them. They appeared in the Saturday Review under the name of Norman Cousins. This is what he said on this point:
The vital alternative-
That is to national suicide or national survival-
-is a massive attempt through the United Nations to relate the crisis of Berlin to the larger crisis facing the world. That larger crisis is represented by the^ absence of effective law in the relationships of nations, and the likelihood of aggression in a situation in which nations are allowed to decide for themselves what their security requires.
Mr. Khrushchev has warned that he will not be intimidated by what the United Nations may decide. If this is the case, then this should be the central issue, rather than Berlin alone. If the Soviet wishes to take the position that it is stonily opposed to any attempt to settle differences among nations on the basis of world law and world will, then the entire human community should consider the implications of this fact. In any event,

Supply-External Affairs
the issue of Berlin is not just whether the United States is right or the Soviet union is right. The issue is whether the contending nations have the right to proceed without regard for the lives and opinions of others. Mankind is involved and mankind has a right to be consulted. There can be no more hideous arrogance than is represented by a policy that involves other peoples without their fullest participation in any determination.
Not until the United Nations is made central in any attack on the Berlin problem, and not until the power of world public opinion is tapped, can we or anyone say that the only alternative to Soviet intransigence in Berlin is nuclear force.
You may say, Mr. Chairman, that this is vague idealism. Well, perhaps it is, but surely it is the only kind of thing in the long run, which can save us from annihilation. Last night the hon. member for Niagara Falls said that "Canada has no preordained destiny." Our destiny will be what we deserve and work for. Well, Canada has no preordained destiny; neither has the world. Our destiny in the world is what we make it, and we can make it today, if we so desire, one which will make possible the good life for all people beyond the dreams of all previous generations, or we can make it a wasteland of ruin and destruction. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, and I conclude with his words, "We are on the brink".

Mr. Chairman, I regard it as an honour as well as a responsibility to take a part, however small, in this debate which deals with matters of such inexpressible gravity. We have just listened to a speech from a highly respected member of this house who has experience beyond almost any of us in external affairs. He talked plainly with no attempt to conceal the gravity of the situation we face.
As I listened yesterday to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has worked so assiduously on these questions since he took on his present job and has come to know so much of the world, I was struck with the fact of the grave words he used. I should like to quote a few of them because he is calling on us to make efforts and sacrifices such as we have known in the past. In fact he calls on us as possibly having to do things that we knew only in wartime. We have never learned, so far as I can discover, that the state deserves any service in peacetime such as we gave in wartime. I should now like to read a word or two from what the minister said yesterday as to the challenge we face. He said, as reported in the Globe and Mail of this morning:
Perhaps we have had enough of the soft life anyway. But the road ahead is certainly going to be hard and there will be tension for a long, long time. We might just as well face that fact. From Canadians courage will be required, both physical


and moral, and sacrifice, and I believe above all, a return to our deep abiding fundamental faiths. If we face this challenge we will win through.
I also wish to refer to the speech made last Saturday, I think it was, by the Prime Minister to the bar association because I welcomed so greatly what he said then. It seemed to me he gave a very much needed lead all over the world when he said quite frankly that we could not expect everything we wanted. He said that we should not expect to gain all our ends. Any final solution he said, is bound to contain "certain elements distasteful to the west" as well as "features unpalatable to the U.S.S.R." One of the things I want to say today-I hope perhaps it may win some hearing-is that I think we have got into the habit of dividing the world into two kinds of people, people who believe in the capitalist system and are good and people who believe in the socialist or communist system and are bad. I think this is a wholly artificial and even childish attitude.
Within the last generation we have worked twice with the Russians in wartime, and were we glad to have them. It almost seems a perversity of fate that we now find ourselves in the position in which we are. Nevertheless I hope we will never despair and I see no reason to despair. Even today there comes some encouragement. I think the interview between Khrushchev and the United States journalist, Sulzberger, shows that there is more than a ray of hope. If Khrushchev had said, "We can smash you all to pieces and we are going to be sitting pretty", I would have been worried. I have not read the full text but I understand Khrushchev said, in effect, "We will both be smashed up". That statement seems to me a great step forward.
I always have it in the back of my mind that Khrushchev, like everyone else in such a position, may be doing a certain amount of bluffing and that he may even occasionally have a quiet laugh at the consternation he is causing. After the interview he gave to Sulzberger, no one will make me believe that he is going to push off with all the chances that pressing the button would carry.
I am not going to attempt to discuss high political questions or questions of strategy. I am not sufficiently versed in them and I think they have been dealt with adequately. All I aim to do today is to say some things which perhaps may win credence as to what the ordinary man should be doing at this time and where people who are not in government, who are not in diplomacy, just ordinary guys, you might say, living their lives, come into the picture. I should like to speak along that line.
I like to look back. I was thinking today of the irony of the situation. I, unfortunately,

can look back to 1914. I remember how we thanked God tor the Russians. I remember what terrible anxieties we went through when they cracked up in the winter of 1917. As I read the lives ot the leaders of those days I realize that I did not understand the terrible strains they were under in the winter of 1917-18 before we had the great German attack in March. That was our experience with the Russians and it was the same again in the second world war after a false start, if you like. Nevertheless, you will remember what Churchill said about them when they entered the conflict. He said in effect that he might not approve of everything they did but they were good soldiers and we were glad to have them. That is a free paraphrase of what he said but that is its effect and we certainly were glad to have them.
Then we came to the time after the war and we encountered ideological difficulties which were so great, and which we have allowed to become so decisive. I sometimes wonder whether we have needed to allow them to become so great. I am going to make a great confession. I have socialist friends. I go and have dinner in their houses. Apparently there are certain kinds of socialists who are not respectable but I do not think their viewpoint prevails too much in our Canadian thinking. As I read United States publications, however, I sometimes wonder where their tirades are taking them.
I think we should remind ourselves that we are talking about ideologies. For some centuries the Protestants and the Catholics tore each other to pieces. They were all good Christians but they were busy tearing each other to pieces. They do not do it so much now. We have learned how to live together and I think we have got to learn something from that experience so far as our relations with the Russians are concerned. In my opinion it is terribly important that we should. My friend asks me if that includes Presbyterians. I realize that Presbyterians are a tough breed but I think it does. I think there is a basis of reasonableness in a Presbyterian if you pursue it far enough.
It is a long pursuit.

Well, between the Baptists and the Presbyterians it may be about 50-50. I want to introduce a word which I understand has become almost a naughty word in the United States, the word "coexistence". Apparently it has now come to mean almost the same as appeasement which, of course, was a very naughty word in the 30's particularly. I want to take the word "coexistence" and ask hon. members to consider what it means. We know, of course, what it means, literally. In plain words it just means living together.
