I was interested to find that that great historian Toynbee, who surveys the centuries in the same way most of us look back on last week, makes this comment which I think is worth reading. It is quite short and I believe it is profoundly true. He said:
Now for the first time in history the whole human race has been united on the military plane.
That, I suppose, is true and if it is true it is a truth that affects all of us profoundly- the whole world united on the military plane. You can go on from that and argue that in view of that fact there is only one thing for the world to do and that is to become united on other planes. At any rate, in the meantime surely any sensible person is entitled to say "coexistence".
What does coexistence mean? First of all I think it means that we recognize that we are not always in the right. In my opinion that is important. We are extremely critical of the Russians now because they make rather devastating remarks about us, our way of life, our society, and what they are going to do to us, but let us not forget that for a long time, particularly after the first war when socialism and communism were young, we were very high and mighty. We proclaimed to the world that they never could succeed and in fact we treated them with a good deal of disdain. It is not altogether surprising that they take a critical view of us. Nevertheless, do not forget that even after all that, when the second war came and common sense prevailed we urged them to join us and they did join us and were of great help, as we know.
I feel that coexistence implies two things. As I have tried to say, it implies give and take. As the Prime Minister said, it does not mean that we should always get our own way. It does not mean that we think we are always right. In his speech I thought the Prime Minister was very wise in abandoning the pretense that everything we did was right and that if there were negotiations we must get everything and give nothing. I am not at all sure that he has not already had some influence in the world diplomacy as a result of that speech.
I am glad to see that Khrushchev, whatever his motives are, is again suggesting negotiation and also, as I said a moment ago, he is not pretending that if the ultimate evil came Russia would come out of it easily. As I said, coexistence implies two things, the first being give and take. In the second place, it implies that we believe that there are certain good things that the other people have, certain things from which we can learn, certain things which our way of life can get from them, certain ways in which we can associate happily with each other. I feel there should be

Supply-External Affairs far more of that kind of thing than there is. Suppose you could imagine such a state of affairs, as the thought which occurred to me this morning, that a group of mad men got into power in Canada and in the United States and set out to bring the two countries to war. I think the citizens of Canada and United States would sit back and laugh at them. I know that is a fantastic suggestion but I am only making it because it seems to me we should not pretend to ourselves that there is no use having anything to do with the individual Russian, that he does not count.
There was a popular play many years ago involving a little principality on the northwest frontier of India. A highly sophisticated and educated Cambridge man-there are educated Cambridge men-was the head of the principality. A brutal and horrible religious ceremony was going to take place. One of his Cambridge friends said, "Surely you are not going to stand by and let that kind of thing happen". "Look", he said, "even the most absolute monarch depends on the consent of the governed. My rule would not last 24 hours if I tried to stop it." That is what he said and I am not at all sure there is not a basic truth in it. When people say that the Russians are ready to rebel it is never very convincing to me. Incidentally, if I may digress for a moment I should like to refer to a very interesting letter which I commend to everyone in this chamber. It was from a man in Moscow. It was addressed to the Globe and Mail which was sporting enough to publish it. It was quite an attack on the Globe and Mail or an editorial in the Globe and Mail. As I remember it, the editorial was headed "The Servile State". In any event the word "servile" was in it. I took this article to the publisher. I did not see him but I left a message for him congratulating him on publishing the editorial and saying, "I want you to read that editorial. I think you will find a good many things in it for you and me to answer". This letter was reasonably written and was really an attempt to answer the suggestion that in Russia they were being tyrannized over and that they hated what was happening. I do not think we can believe that is the situation. You cannot give the figures as to Russian increase in production, as to what they have done in the realm of science which we used to jeer at not so many years ago, without having the feeling that these are people of great achievement.
What I wish to say and to get across is what can be done by the ordinary man. We have in this country many people who know a great deal about Russian civilization. I think of the people who are interested in music, in the ballet and in art. They know a

great deal about those matters. They surpass the rest of us, including myself, who know almost nothing about these matters. Should we not face the situation if we believe in coexistence. As it was put by a friend of mine the other day, it is a question of coexistence or no existence. That remark is worth thinking about. I wish I had thought of it myself. If that it true-and I am speaking of the ordinary citizen-we cannot leave public relations just to the few hard pressed people who are bearing the heavy burden of government.
When you come to think of what should be done you may say, "Well, is anything going to be done?" The answer is, no, nothing is going to be done unless we are greatly concerned. Speeches have been made in this house which would indicate that those who made the speeches would be ready to do a great deal.
A few things that can obviously be suggested that should be done of course, are that the universities should do much more for Russian learning, that we should have more Russian music, although of course, we have a great deal. We are already playing games with Russians. The drama, of course, is a common feature. The other thing, of course, is the press. We should know more about Russia. Our press should do more, our radio should do more. I come back again to this very simple argument: Do you believe that over the years we need to practice this coexistence? You may say that it is extremely difficult at the moment when the Russians seem to spend most of their time proclaiming that we are warmongers. I admit that it is extremely hard to put up with that sort of thing when we know how unsound it is. But then it seems to me that it would not need tens of thousands of people coming here but rather it would need only a reasonable number of intelligent Russian tourists coming to this country to find out that all this talk about our wanting war is crazy, and that this propaganda is crazy. I understand that in some of the eastern countries, when television got out there and they saw for the first time the kind of life that we were really living here, they were no longer content to put up with the kind of economic existence they were having. I mention that matter merely because I am trying very hard to suggest what can be done by the ordinary person who goes about his business, who is a decent fellow to live with and who would probably think that he could no more have influence on what is happening in Russia than he could fly to heaven. But I suggest that these things could be done and should be done; and that once we could get across the idea that the people

in Russia and the people in Canada are not so very different, it might have its effect. My mind went back today to those lines by Rudyard Kipling with respect to Tommy Atkins. Tommy is soliloquizing:
For it's Tommy this, an' Tommy that, an' "Chuck 'im out, the brute!"
But it's "Thank you Mr. Atkins" when the guns begin to shoot.
Then somewhere else he makes Tommy Atkins say:
We ain't no blood red 'eroes And we ain't no black guards too But single men in barricks Most remarkable like you.
That is a trivial thing to introduce into this solemn assembly but somehow or other it seems that if we could get across the idea that these people in Russia are people very much like ourselves and if we could somehow have it brought home to us in the press and so on, I believe it might have some effect.
These are trivial and rather obvious thoughts that I have tried to express. The only excuse for them is that I believe that not one tenth of 1 per cent of the people in the country at this time have ever thought there was any duty on them to take any part. They thought that it should be left to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition who know about these things. It is true that they know about these things and are doing the best they can. However, it seems to me that the ordinary Canadian citizen is deeply concerned in this matter and that he has a duty to find out if there is anything he can do about the matter. I suggest with some confidence that our universities, churches, newspapers, theatres and ballet could do something, if somehow we could get across to them the idea that they are great makers of public opinion, that here is a job to be done and that coexistence is not a matter for a month or a year but is a continuing matter. It is a matter of a way of life and particularly when we consider the countries that are on balance. I think it was Chester Bowles who recorded that some Indian statesman had said to him. "You people in the west are on trial. It is going to be a question whether you or the communists can do most to help with economic problems in the underdeveloped countries. Don't you people lose out". I sometimes think of what we would feel like if some fine day we found that India had decided to incline the other way. However, that is another matter and it is no time to be introducing it now. I have been glad to have a small part in this debate.

In this debate some distinguished speakers have taken part. The subject is the gravest one that I think the house can face. As a rather humble backbencher I
Supply-External Affairs venture to speak in the hope that I may add something to the debate. By way of preface I may say that I intend to be somewhat critical of western foreign policy as it has been followed for some time. I am not entirely convinced that I am correct and that everyone else is wrong. However, I am much buoyed up by that theory of argument that if I am wrong, then perhaps the right policy will be shown up and be proven even more right by contrast with it. I feel that I must be critical because, in my opinion to date, western policy has not been too successful. There are two pieces of evidence I think that back me up in this opinion. One is the present world situation in which we are on the brink of war. The second is the fact that over the last few years communism, a system that we have despised, hated and fought so strongly against, has been able to make such great inroads and such great progress in the rest of the world.
First, as to the matter of brink of war or the situation today, may I say this. I have been alarmed by some of the speeches made in the house and by speaking with some people across the country who talk so calmly about the possibility of war. Every time you mention the possibility of war they seem to give you the answer, "Well, what are you going to do? Give in to the communists?"
I do not think it is a simple matter of one or the other. I think that either one is unthinkable. Of course, the task of diplomacy today is to make sure that both are avoided. However, I do believe-and here is where I differ with many of my friends-that the possibility of war today is worse than communism.
Frankly, what we fear about communism is that were we to become subjected to that system we would lose so many of those things we treasure so much; our freedom, our democratic system and all those wonderful things we have been able to gain in modern civilization, mostly because we have had the benefits of that system.
However, I do not think we gain much by comparing the present situation to the days before the last world war or by talking about appeasement. If there were a war today we would lose much more than we could possibly lose to the communists. If there were a war I am convinced there would be no vestige of civilization left in the world. If humanity could survive at all, I think the disruption of ordinary life would be so great that there would be no type of ordered government whatsoever and we would have the most horrible of all situations in human affairs, complete anarchy. All that would straighten

Supply-External Affairs out that situation would be a regimentation so tight and so severe that communism would be benevolent in comparison.
Surely we cannot take so lightly the possibility of our blind fight against communism leading us into a danger of something even greater, talk about it or even think about the possibility. Surely it is the time to stop and look. Instead of merely saying, "What nasty fellows those communists are", we should say, "Have we done everything we can to protect ourselves and the rest of the world from this frightening holocaust that threatens us?"
I am buoyed up somewhat in my critical attitude by the thought that today there are some 25 uncommitted nations in the world which refuse to join what I call the anticommunist bloc; which are not on our side in the cold war. Surely if after the amounts of money this house has voted, after the extreme gestures of generosity made by the western world toward new and emerging nations, the amounts of money poured in on foreign aid and programs of one type and another, those 25 nations are still unwilling to join us, it could be just possible that our conduct and our character have not been so blameless and so spotless that we should not look critically at ourselves.
I firmly believe that perhaps the most basic error we have made is in being anti-communist first and pro-democratic second. We have seen examples of this in the manner in which some tottering regimes have been bolstered up in the Far East, for instance, where the first test seems to have been. What is the position of these people who are fighting for power on each side in this country? Which group is the most anti-communist? Which group would make the greatest contribution to our side in terms of power against the communists?" Then we pour in the money.
Surely the question that should occur to the minds of Christian, democratic people, should be, "How best can we help these people to achieve those things that they lack? How best can we help them secure a form of government that will give them the most they can obtain of those things that we treasure most?"
I suggest it has been this course of conduct, this indiscriminate choosing of allies that has caused some of the uncommitted nations to be somewhat sceptical of our methods and to appear downright ungrateful for such assistance as we have given them.
Today I think that Russia is afraid of us, as we are afraid of her. There is no doubt in my mind, having looked at the type of immigrants of various races from around the world that we have in this country, that basically the citizens of Russia, Japan, China, Poland or Britain are not that much different.

I think it is not just the western world and the citizens of their countries that are deathly afraid of war, but the citizens of all countries around the world.
I suggest that if those uncommitted nations are suspicious of our methods and our actions when we have been trying to help them, surely it should be understandable why Russia, which has been the object of our anticommunism, should find herself so unwilling to believe we are at all sincere in our protestations for peace and our saying that we do not mean her any harm. It seems to me there are a few common misconceptions which, while they may have been mentioned now and then, are not taken seriously enough into consideration or do not underly our thinking if we are really trying to find a peaceful solution.
First, the hon. member for Greenwood mentioned coexistence. It is a peculiarity of the thinking today, in the United States particularly, that to mention the word "coexistence" puts one sort of into the appeasement class or that of a fellow traveller. Let us look at it very realistically. The communists are there in many countries. Their system is well and firmly entrenched. They are extremely powerful.
There is more than that. There is no doubt that they have the solid support of a large segment of their population. In fact, we can see no reasonable hope that in the very near future they are likely to be overthrown. They are there. They are strong. They are going to remain there unless they can be overthrown by force of arms and, as I said before, I think that any question of overthrow by force of arms means we will be out of the frying pan and into the fire. It cannot be done without destroying us all.
Therefore peaceful coexistence is the only existence there is. It is not an alternate form of action; it is the only possibility. Therefore we must do all we can to try to relieve the tension which might destroy us all. Certainly if we are going to live in peace with our neighbours it would behove us to have a foreign policy more in keeping with our Christian, democratic principles than merely an anti-communist line.
I am all too familiar with an American saying which seems to underly much of their thinking. It was almost a battle cry before the last world war. That saying is, "Make the world safe for democracy". In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, there can be no more dangerous expression. Democracy, by its very nature, can never be safe. It is an idea of government, an ideology. As such it is always going to be under attack by all other ideologies. In fact, by its very nature, in order to work properly it must always allow all other ideologies full

scope and full discussion. Our concept of democracy is not a symbol which can be put up like a flag and held just so. Our concept of democracy today may be vastly different from that which may evolve in 20 years time. Anti-communist policy tends to make our policies all become rigid, and a democracy that becomes rigid leaves itself without its own greatest defence, the fact that it is pliable and can bend to meet all emergencies.
Democracy cannot stand still. It cannot be solid and unbending. It cannot become so dedicated to something like anti-communism that the ordinary citizens in the street are afraid to talk about our way of life in comparison with the communist system. Once we start to do that, we lose any chance of improving our own system. When we lose any chance of improving our own system, we give a chance to the communists whom we are trying very hard to defeat. It seems strange to me that whereas communism is supposed to be a very rigid thing it has throughout the world evolved and changed enough to enable it to keep ahead of us. We have had many manifestations of the extent to which anti-communism will go in our country and the harm it can do to democracy. One example, for instance, is McCarthyism. We can lose, by our own anti-communist struggle, that which we are trying to preserve for ourselves.
We want democracy because it gives us a freedom of action, freedom of speech, freedom of choice and religion. The more we try to channel our efforts into a policy which can only be based on fear and hatred of communism, then the more effectively do we strangle those things which are finest in our own civilization. I believe that in the present world situation not only is it possible for the west and the east to have a war that can destroy civilization, but that any country which has a sufficient stockpile of nuclear arms and the means to deliver them can stand on its own two feet. I do not believe the United States needs any backers in its own defence. Who would dare attack her? There would be no possibility of winning such a war because certainly the amount of destruction would be far greater than any possible gains. Consequently, the United States must feel quite safe standing on its own two feet. The United Kingdom and France are in the same situation.
When we are trying to explain to these uncommitted nations, or in fact to Russia, that our alliances are only defensive alliances and not aimed against Russia, we can at least understand why the Russians fear those alliances. Living in this country as we do and knowing our fellow citizens so well
Supply-External Affairs we sometimes forget that while we are perfectly sure of our motives and our aims, while we know we have so much that we need not look with greed on anyone else's possession, while we have been treated so well by nature and have had so few real enemies, most peoples in the world have not had the advantage of growing up as we have. They cannot take our aims and motives for granted as we do. They cannot even judge them as critically as we do. When I say it is difficult for them to look at our alliances and realize the purpose is only defensive and not offensive and that, for the reasons I have just explained, one country can stand alone and we have banded together for defensive purposes, I mean that even on the basis of western reasoning we can understand why there would be confusion.
I think we too often forget that there are language barriers and other differences in the way in which these people have grown up and lived, differences in the meaning of a word. When one adds all these things together one finds there is a basis for understanding that at least the Russians might have a very real fear of us. There is no doubt, I think, in the minds of most members of this house that we are afraid of the Russians. We have heard their pronouncements about spreading world communism. We do know that they have tried to infiltrate other countries. We do know we have reason to fear communists and the spread of communism. Surely we can understand, therefore, that if we are afraid, they are honestly afraid. If both sides are afraid of a world war, then fear is going to be the complicating factor in negotiations which, while not making it impossible, will make it most difficult to arrive at any solution to our problems.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the western world now has more than sufficient arms and armaments to destroy the Russian world ten times over. I cannot forget that at the end of the last world war we were subjected to V-2 attacks from Germany that were fairly accurate. This was at a time when rockets were practically unknown and there was only 1,000 pounds of t.n.t. in the warhead. Since that time we have had sputniks which have gone into space around the moon. Surely, there cannot be much doubt that there are probably enough intercontinental ballistic missiles stockpiled on either side of the iron curtain to blast the other half of the world. I suggest it is not necessary, therefore, for us to continue to pile proof upon proof of how strong we are and how determined we are.
If, as I suggest, the most difficult factor in negotiations is really fear and not this truculence, then we are only piling fear upon fear.

Supply-External Affairs Could we not afford to make some real gesture by unilaterally dropping some part of our armanent and saying to Russia, "Here, we will start this way." I do not believe we would be exposing ourselves to that much danger. I think we need to show in very concrete form which even the most complex oriental mind can comprehend that our purpose is not aggression. I feel this is part of the reason we have been unable to sell some of the uncommitted nations on our story, and why we do not have the full support of the well meaning nations in the world.
What we have failed to understand is not just the Russian mind but the minds of the members of the new nations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned that these people were too busy with their own problems. This may be one way of putting it, but I should like to say that their problems really should be our first preoccupation. Their welfare and democracy have not been developed as they have in this country. They must strive for such development. They cannot equate, as some people seem to, the concept of the defeat of communism with the gaining of democracy. Those who fought in world war II know that there are other menaces to democracy. Not long ago we fought a war against the Nazis. There are in existence in the world today dictatorships of various kinds. I am sure the United States should have learned a lesson from Cuba, the lesson being that when you have one bad master you do not really fear the possibility of another as much as you fear the one you have. If we are to really achieve peaceful coexistence we must get rid of some of these misconceptions in our thinking.
I do not believe Russia wants war. I started out by saying that the communists have been making great progress without war. I am sure they realize as clearly as we do that war will mean not gain but only destruction. Therefore, since they appear to have such confidence in their system, I honestly believe they would really like to achieve and maintain peace, although perhaps peace on their terms. We do not aid the cause of peace by striving with all our might and bending all our energies in an anti-communist drive. We have not been successful in anticommunist campaigns. There is only one course for us to follow and that is for us to be prodemocracy. The purer democracy is the stronger it will be and the safer we will be. Many of my colleagues have suggested that this is a highly idealistic approach. They say that is all very well but we are dealing with a very nasty fellow. All I can say is that this has always been said any time a danger to democracy has reared its head.


I am one of those who happen to believe that the purer we keep democracy the safer we are. The more above criticism we keep our own actions-the more Christianlike our actions-the less chance there will be of making enemies and certainly there will be less distrust of us. We have to have peaceful coexistence or no existence as was just said. We must begin by removing as much of the fear as we can. Part of the task before us is to remove distrust which can be removed if we are more devoted Christian democrats. I hope that our foreign policy may start to be more prodemocratic and less anti-communist, and I am sure we will have fewer communists.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, it is with a certain amount of trepidation that I rise to take part in this debate because it is my misfortune to follow in the debate such political giants and eloquent statesmen as the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member for Essex East and the Leader of the Opposition.
Yesterday in his calm, cool and collected manner, the minister gave us a most graphic picture of present day world conditions. The hon. member for Essex East who followed, although in different words, made a no less sincere effort to warn Canadians and the people of the free world of the dangers we now face. The Leader of the Opposition whose knowledge of foreign affairs is beyond question delivered an outstanding address which greatly impressed the committee and will, I am sure, impress all Canadians. All hon. members who have participated in the debate have contributed a great deal in placing on the record the thinking of Canadians.
Before entering the chamber yesterday I read an article written by an eminent journalist and reporter who is read by most hon. members of this committee and whose opinion is highly valued. I wish to quote a portion of the article:
It may be that Canadian foreign policy debates fail to impress because few, if any, of the participants have anything of real importance to say. Canadian foreign policy is often a pale reflection of foreign policies devised elsewhere.
Upon reading that portion of the article I was led to expect that I would not be impressed by the debate but I have no hesitation in saying that I have been greatly impressed. Previously I was inclined to feel that probably our foreign policy was dictated by others and by circumstances beyond our control but after hearing the masterful addresses of those who have preceded me in the debate I have altered my thinking. This debate impressed me as I am sure it did all hon.

members of the committee. Undoubtedly it will impress the millions of Canadians who are carefully watching to ascertain what foreign policy Canada is following.
The author of this article attempted to guess what was going to happen. If he had regard for Canada's obligations as a full-fledged member of NATO, as a member of the British Commonwealth of Nations and as one of the bastions of the free world then certainly he would have known that our foreign policy could not be completely original because it must have regard for and be co-ordinated with the lines of the policies of our allies and associates. On the other hand it is by no means a pale reflection of policies devised elsewhere. What we have heard expressed in the debate is a dynamic, purely Canadian policy dictated by the difficult circumstances that presently exist.
There is another aspect of the debate which greatly impressed me as I am sure it did all Canadians. We saw a spectacle in this house which is a rarity, and which appears only on infrequent occasions. I refer to the fact that we have a bipartisan foreign policy. I hope I am using the right word. It was a spectacle which I had not had the privilege of seeing since I had the honour of coming to this house in 1957. It was a spectacle where the government and the official opposition, in spite of their political differences, closed ranks in time of crisis. All of those who spoke before me agreed with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we do live in a time of crisis. However, it is regrettable that we have not a tripartisan foreign policy, since there are still a few people who would scrap the policy we are Canada declare its complete neutrality, have following, who would scrap NATO and have Canada betray its allies, its friends. Oh, what a comfort it would be to those who threaten our freedom.
Neutrality is a very attractive word, Mr. Chairman. I have heard it outside this house. But history teaches us otherwise. Did neutrality pay off in the last war to countries such as Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Norway and others? Some people in Canada, intentionally or otherwise, misinterpret the objects and aims of NATO, why this organization was created and on what basis. Why was it necessary 10 or 12 years ago, and why is it necessary today. This country knows, and every member of the NATO organization knows, why this alliance was created. It was created purely for defensive purposes and it stands on those aims today. Let us recall history; let us go back, Mr. Chairman. It was created to stem the tide of communist dictatorship which inundated central Europe and threatened to
Supply-External Affairs complete the conquest of the whole of western Europe. If NATO had not come into existence it is almost a certainty that there would not be a free nation in Europe today in the sense that we understand freedom. Those behind the iron curtain understand freedom differently; they understand democracy differently, but I wager that there would not be a free nation in Europe today. And yet we have people who say "scrap NATO", or who ask Canada to get out of NATO. I know hon. members will agree with me; I know I am making a correct statement.
NATO is a defensive alliance. Does it threaten the red empire? Let us look at the facts. Neither NATO nor any one of its member nations has ever in the past 10 or 12 years since its inception displayed any imperialistic designs on each other or on the red empire behind the iron curtain. Neither NATO nor any one of the member nations of NATO has, in the words of Mr. Khrushchev, "threatened to bury" the communist ideology. However, we have heard from the mouth of the great comrade Khrushchev that he was going to bury us. He made that statement in the United States, but he included us as well. Oh, how he would like to break up the friendship that exists between our two great countries.
We have not made any plans to, and it is not our policy to bury the ideology which is foreign to us, which is unpalatable to us, which is disgusting to us and which we do not wish to accept. Each member of NATO pledged itself to come to the assistance of the other only if attacked, but not to attack first.
I think the Soviets are right when they say that Canadians are peace loving people. All the peoples of every free nation in NATO are peace loving and want peace. They are striving for it. NATO does not threaten the peace or security of the great red empire. There is no incident in history which shows that we threaten the red empire; it is not in our planning. Each member-this includes Canada- knows what threats communism poses to its very existence, to its way of life, to its democratic system of government, to its system of justice and freedom of religion and the press.
I cannot understand how the Soviet bosses believe that NATO is a threat. They warned Greece against allowing certain manoeuvres in the Mediterranean. They threatened to take certain repressive actions if Greece did not get out of the NATO alliance. But NATO does not build 15-foot walls to keep its people in even if they wish to go behind the iron curtain. Look at the thousands and thousands who have crossed the line at the risk of their lives and have abandoned all their worldly possessions to cross into West Berlin. Let us

Supply-External Affairs not forget the thousands and thousands of refugees who have found a home in Canada, who refuse to be repatriated, who refuse to go back. Is there not a reason for this? Have we any such situation in our NATO organization? Why, Mr. Chairman, the NATO organization has been so accommodating that some people think it has gone too far in trying to allay the fears of the communist empire. It has gone so far as to write off the peoples who are behind the iron curtain and who were once free. There is nothing in the policies of NATO to free or help these people to gain their freedom. A typical example, probably the best of all, is the Hungarian uprising in 1956 when not even a finger was raised in defence of these people who were crushed by Russian tanks. The same fate will await any other peoples who dare to rebel against the regime set up by Moscow.
In the opinion of many, NATO may rue the day that it did not adopt as one segment of its policy the freeing of these enslaved peoples. Mr. Khrushchev dares to talk about colonialism. We have become very complacent. We would be so happy to be left alone that we are not concerned about any enslaved nation. We go along with Mr. Khrushchev, with internal domestic policy of the Soviet union, and it is none of our business. We may rue the day that NATO did not threaten the dismemberment of the Soviet union and its great empire, but NATO is a stumbling block in the spread of that godless ideology and it is that stumbling block that hurts. It is not fear that we are going to attack them. We are a strictly defensive alliance. We would not condone or approve any overt action by any of our allies that would start a shooting war. We are a peace loving nation.
I know that colonialism is in the minds of the newly liberated countries as they have been called. Mr. Khrushchev is certainly fostering a spirit of hate, a spirit of revenge in those lands even against so-called benevolent oppressors such as the British empire. But how about his own empire? There is only one head of state so far who has dared to raise his voice on behalf of the enslaved peoples of Europe. That head of state is the head of a member nation of NATO, and he did so in New York on September 26, 1960. I refer to that great address by the Prime Minister of Canada to the United Nations. May I be permitted, Mr. Chairman, to quote a portion of his address. It was reported in the newspapers but I think it deserves to go into the permanent records of parliament.
Indeed in this assembly the membership is composed in a very considerable measure of the graduates of empires, mandates and trusteeships of the United Kingdom, the commonwealth and other nations. I pause to ask this question: How many

human beings have been liberated by the U.S.S.R.? Do we forget how one of the post-war colonies of the U.S.S.R. sought to liberate itself four years ago, and with what results?
It is almost five years ago now.
I say that because these facts of history in the commonwealth and other countries invite comparison with the domination over peoples and territories, sometimes gained under the guise of liberation, but always accompanied by the loss of political freedom. How are we to reconcile the tragedy of the Hungarian uprising in 1956 with Chairman Khrushchev's confident assertion of a few days ago in this assembly? Mr. Khrushchev said: "It has been and always will be our stand that the peoples of Africa, like those of other continents striving for their liberation from the colonial yoke, should establish orders in their countries of their own will and choice.'' That I accept, and I hope that those words mean a change of attitude for the future on the part of those he represents.
What of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia? What of the freedom loving Ukrainians and many other eastern European peoples which I shall not name for fear of omitting some of them? Mr. Khrushchev went further and said: "Complete and final elimination of the colonial regime in all its forms and manifestations has been prompted by the entire course of world history in the last decades." There can be no double standard in international affairs. I ask the chairman of the council of ministers of the U.S.S.R. to give to those nations under his domination the right of free elections.
All the Prime Minister suggested was giving these people the right of free elections. What did he receive in reply? Desk beating with the boot of the dictator, and the Soviet press with the attitude of a mad dog raked the Prime Minister of Canada over the coals, criticized him and said that it was none of his business, that it was purely a matter of the domestic policy of the Soviet union.
What objection could anyone have to free elections in any one of these states? We are not concerned about what form of government Yugoslavia might choose. We would not be concerned about what form of government Poland, Roumania, Lithuania, Bulgaria and other such countries would establish within their own boundaries as long as it was done through free choice. We would like to know whether Czechoslovakians would vote in favour of the communist regime and to remain as a satellite or colony of Moscow. We would like to know the opinion of these peoples with respect to the domestic policy of this great empire, a domestic policy with which we have not tried to interfere and as to which Mr. Khrushchev says it is none of our business.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-39, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to move the second reading of Bill No. C-39, an act to amend the Railway Act, the explanatory note of which states:
The purpose of this amendment is to provide that representatives of the trucking industry shall have the right to make application to the board of transport commissioners for the disallowance of a competitive rate when they consider that such rate has subjected motor vehicle operators to an undue or unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage.
From these explanatory notes that are contained in the bill one might come to the conclusion that this amendment was strictly in the interests of the trucking industry. However, that is not the main purpose of the bill, which is to provide protection for the public interest in regard to freight rates. I say that because the railways in 1957 started some substantial rate reductions by way of what are called truck competitive rates or incentive rates. In some instances, in the western incentive rates that were put into effect in 1957 by the railway, those reductions amounted to as much as 75 per cent of the rate that was then in effect. It is to be realized that it was the advent of truck competition that brought about those reductions. Of course, there should be no objection to the public benefiting from those reductions. However, I think we want to have the safeguard that the railway is not going to be allowed now to reduce the rates to an uneconomic level and therefore put out of business the very firms which brought about these freight rates reductions in the first instance. That is something that has happened very notably in one section of the trucking industry, and I am very conscious of this matter, coming as I do from the province of British Columbia.
The trucking industry started up in the business of hauling automobiles from the plants at Windsor and Oshawa out to Vancouver and they brought about substantial
Railway Act
reductions in the cost of bringing an automobile out to Vancouver and to other parts of British Columbia. Then the railways were allowed to enter into agreed charges which practically eliminated that section of the trucking industry. Some 50 firms started up in that business and, as I say, brought about substantial reductions in the cost of moving an automobile to Vancouver, and they were eliminated by means of the agreed charges. In other instances, other parts of the trucking industry are threatened by these incentive rates and truck competitive rates.
The act at the present time-and I refer to section 334 of the Railway Act-contains certain safeguards. It provides that the railways must charge compensatory rates and that they must not go beyond the cost to the railway to move those goods. However, in the various hearings that have taken place over the years it has been clearly established that, with the number of competitive and incentive rates that are now coming into effect-and I know that a number of years ago there were 30,000 of them-and in the establishing of those 30,000 rates, the railways had beeen questioned some three or four times by the board of transport commissioners as to whether or not those rates were compensatory. They were only asked for information on those three or four occasions. It did not appear to me or, I think, to most of those involved in the hearing, that this was causing any substantial hardship to the railways. However, the Canadian National Railways in particular have protested very strenuously against these restrictions, as they call them. In fact they asked the present royal commission on transportation to eliminate any such restrictions so that they would not be required to show that their rates would be compensatory and so that they could in effect charge any rates they wanted to charge.
In actual fact the railways already have full scope for setting rates to meet their competition and rightly so. I am sure that we would not want to put the railways in a position in which they could not meet their competition. But in view of the large subsidies that are being paid by the Canadian taxpayers to the railway, I feel that we want to have some safeguard in order to make sure that the railways are not engaging in unfair competition. That is why I suggest that this amendment is necessary.
On the face of it, if two industries are on equal terms of course free competition itself would ensure the lowest possible rate to the consumer and that is the ultimate result we want to attain. However, the conditions as between the trucking industry and the rail

Railway Act
industry are not equal by any stretch of the imagination. For one thing, the resources of the railway are far beyond those of the average trucking firm. Even though trucking firms have grown to be a great deal larger than they used to be, they certainly cannot compete with the financial resources of the railways. They could not afford to sustain a loss over a period of time as a railway could do. The railway could charge a low rate from point A to point B for a few months and eliminate truck competition or do as they have been doing over the past year or so, namely buying out trucking firms which are put in an untenable position and are unable to continue. The trucking industry is also faced with that kind of competition; it is faced not only with rail competition but with the competition of the truck lines that are now being acquired by the railroads. I have here a letter which I think went to most members of parliament. It is from a trucking operator in Winnipeg, namely Reimer Express Lines Limited. It is dated June 29, 1961, and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Browne:
Did you know that East-West Transport Ltd., a crown owned, financed, and subsidized truckline, is one of the biggest rate cutters in the business? They are charging rates without regard to operating costs. If this continues, they will succeed in putting taxpayers out of business with remarkable speed.
In view of the apparent losses East-West has had since the Canadian National Railways purchased it, I thought this would be of interest to you.
It is signed by D. S. Reimer, vice president and general manager. As to the part to which he refers there, namely the apparent losses of East-West Transport, this was confirmed in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping when there was produced last year by the hon. member for Port Arthur a document which indicated quite clearly that the trucking operations of the Canadian National for the most part had suffered a substantial loss. It was only the inclusion of one large firm which had made a substantial profit which was able to bring them into a position where they said they did not lose any money in their over-all trucking operations. However, the fact is that several truck lines owned and operated by the railway were engaging in competition with private enterprise and were operating at uneconomical rates.
In this country we have always stressed the benefits of private enterprise. I think we are getting into a dangerous situation. This matter is of concern, of course, to the general public because I am sure that no one in this country wants to see private business put out of existence and replaced by government operated businesses, especially under unfair conditions such as those. It is of course of great concern
[Mr. Browne (Vancouver-Kingsway) .1
to people in the management of trucking industries who have invested their money and to the private citizens in this country who have invested their money in the trucking business which brought about lower freight rates to the people of Canada. They feel they are being discriminated against in the manner in which they are being treated. Of course, the matter is also of great concern to the employees of the trucking industry, of which I might say there are some 90,000. I believe most members of parliament have received representations from some of the unions of the employees of the trucking industry in the last few days. I recall receiving some of them myself last year. In fact, I think I read into the record of Hansard some of the resolutions that had been passed by the various teamster unions across Canada at that time. I went on to point out that the railways and the trucking industry are not on equal terms when it comes to competition because in this fiscal year the railways will receive some $91 million in subsidies from the federal government. In addition to that, Canadian National Railways had a deficit of some $67 million, which is also paid by the Canadian taxpayer. That makes a total of $158 million being paid out of the federal treasury to the railways.
I feel sure that under those circumstances every hon. member of this house would want to ensure that this money is not being used to provide unfair competition with a private enterprise in this country, especially when we consider the fact that the freight rate reductions I have spoken of would never have been brought about without the advent of trucking competition.
I think if the railways are now able to establish that they can cut their rates by as much as 75 per cent we are entitled to ask what kind of rates they were charging before. If they can now cut their rates by 75 per cent and find them to be economical what was the justification for the kind of rates they were charging before? Why should they now be allowed to put out of business those firms which brought about reductions up to that amount?
In many instances there even seems to be some doubt as to the justification for these rates to meet the competition, although that is one of the terms of the Railway Act in section 334, as I have pointed out. That section states that the railways must establish that the competition exists, rates are compensatory and are not lower than necessary to meet the competition.
I have here an article published in the Financial Post of June 3, 1961. It makes a comparison between truck rates and railway

rates on certain new incentive rates which had been published by Canadian National Railways at that time. The article says:
Trucks only handle freight shipments up to about 45,000 pounds. Even at this truck-load limit, the new railway incentive rates are as much as 20 per cent cheaper.
But when certain commodities are heavy and not bulky and, say, 100,000 pounds can be loaded into a boxcar, the railways' new rate could be 50 per cent less than a trucker's "good" rate.
There would seem to be a reduction far below what is necessary to meet competition. Nobody is going to object to the fact that the public will benefit by lower freight rates being in force, provided this is done on a reasonable basis. However, I suggest that if the railways are cutting rates by anything from 50 per cent to 75 per cent, it needs a good deal of explanation to determine why they find it reasonable and economical to cut them to that level. What assurance will we have that if they force their competition out of business they will not immediately put the rates back up and we will find ourselves in the same position as before?
Throughout the years the argument has been put forward that it does not matter too much if a few trucking companies are forced out of business because it is easy for them to start up; there is not a great capital expenditure involved. It has been said that if one company goes out of business, another one will start and we will soon have the same protection. However, I submit that is not the case any longer, because to operate a transcontinental trucking business today does not involve the kind of trucking operations we had in Canada a number of years ago. A number of years ago a man could start up with one or two trucks at a minimum cost and was able to go into business. There are substantial licensing conditions at the present time. One must have a communications system across Canada, such as teletype, in order to control the operations over the vast distances these trucks must now travel. A truck operator must have depots and terminals across the country at which to service his vehicles and in which to store the goods. In addition, the cost of motor vehicles has increased very tremendously since the early days. The large trucks that run across Canada today cost $40,000 a unit.
Therefore one can see it is not so easy as it used to be to start up and get into the trucking business. Even if one is able to meet all the licensing requirements which are in force today, and all the other conditions, he must still raise a very substantial amount of capital. I submit that the argument which has been used in the past is not valid at the present time.
Railway Act
I believe that at the present time the board is limited in its powers to regulate the industry because of the fact that so many rates are being dealt with by the board. Even though they have the power, of their own volition, to investigate rates, there simply is not the time to investigate each one. It is only when a complaint comes before the board that they are really able to deal with that rate.
At the present time the trucking industry is not in a position to appeal to the board of transport commissioners. This was established quite clearly in 1957 in connection with the western incentive rates which, as I said, reduced rail rates by as much as 75 per cent. For the first time the trucking industry became seriously alarmed at the assault the railways were making upon them and appealed to the board of transport commissioners. Before the board went ahead to hear that particular case they decided the trucking industry was not a party under the Railway Act and therefore had no right of appeal to the board of transport commissioners.
The argument has been put forward in some quarters that the trucking industry is not regulated by the board of transport commissioners and therefore should not have the right of appeal. I suggest that is not a valid argument because most of the other people who already have the right of appeal to the board of transport commissioners do not come under that board either. Yet that argument has never been used against them.
The provincial governments, for instance, have the right of appeal to the board of transport commissioners, and a shipper has a right of appeal to the board. Shippers are not controlled by the federal government, and certainly the provincial governments are not controlled by the federal government. In fact if there is any argument at all in that direction it favours the trucking industry, because whether or not the federal government exercises control over the trucking industry, it is in fact the responsibility of the federal government to regulate that industry. This was decided by the privy council in 1955.
The federal government does not choose to exercise that jurisdiction as fully as it might by virtue of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. The federal government constituted the various provincial boards in Canada with federal powers for the purpose of controlling the trucking industry.
I submit that if this is the way the federal government chooses to regulate the trucking industry, that is not the fault of the industry and certainly should not be any bar to its being heard before the board of transport

Railway Act
commissioners. It seems ridiculous that this industry, which is the industry mainly affected by decisions of the board of transport commissioners, should have no access whatsoever to that board.
This bill is similar in nature to one passed by the house in the first half of the session. That bill dealt with agreed charges. At that time all parties unanimously agreed that the trucking industry should have the right of appeal in regard to agreed charges. I submit that the same considerations exist in regard to competitive rates. Because of the vast financial resources of the railways and, as I have pointed out, the subsidies being paid to them by the federal government-that is, by the Canadian taxpayer-I believe it would certainly be in the public interest that the trucking industry should have this right of appeal.
I can assure the house that my purpose in presenting the bill is to insure that the public will have the lowest possible freight rates.
I have no objection whatever to seeing that the railways lower their rates to the lowest possible economic level. In those fields where they are able to operate at lower rates than the trucking industry, then they should be able to have that business, provided they can operate economically at those rates. I think we want to ensure that we are not going to be paying money out of the federal treasury in the form of subsidies or paying annual deficits in order to have the money used to set rates at uneconomic levels.
By the same token, where the trucking industry is the most efficient operator and can operate at the lowest rate to provide its service for the public of this country, then it should be able to have that business and not be cut out of it by unfair competition. I am sure the house will agree with all these considerations. Certainly it is only a very minor consideration that is being asked in this bill. Before any change can or would be made by the board of transport commissioners, it would have to be clearly established that the railroads were doing something not contemplated by the present legislation. In other words, before the board would make any change in any rate or hamper the railways in any way, there would have to be a violation of the existing law.
Surely, it is not too much to ask that the trucking industry, which has done so much to bring about lower freight rates in Canada, should have the right of appeal. I know this is something which has always found favour in both the House of Commons and the other place when it has come to protecting the rights of people and industries in general. Hon. members have always felt these people should have the right of appeal. I am sure

the house will want to give consent to the passage of this measure in order to protect the public and insure the lowest possible freight rates in Canada as well as the most efficient transportation system we can have.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this bill because I believe it to be in the best interests of justice as applied to our transportation system. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) upon bringing this matter to the attention of the house at this time, as well as upon his able presentation. If there is one subject upon which the members of this house are agreed, it is the importance of cheap transportation. This amendment, if adopted, will give an important branch of the transportation industry recognition that it exists for the purpose of serving an ever increasing number of Canadian people. It should, therefore, no longer be looked upon as an unimportant adjunct to our older established methods of transportation, namely the railways and lake shipping.
The trucking industry, from a very small beginning in the twenties, has now attained a status of considerable proportions, with an investment in excess of $1 billion and carrying more than one hundred million tons of merchandise. The Canadian trucking associations of Canada in their submission to the government last June emphasized that the rapid growth of the country and the spectacular progress of technology during recent years had profoundly changed the structure of Canadian transportation services. A serious problem has been created of adjusting transportation policies to meet the new situation created by the public demand for a more efficient and up to date transportation service, such as having goods delivered to your door.
In the first volume of the report of the royal commission on transportation the transformation of the Canadian transportation set-up was summarized in the following words, and I quote from page 26 of that report:
Since the end of world war II, the transportation environment in Canada has been transformed from a monopolistic one, very much dominated by the railways, into a highly competitive one in which a number of different modes of transport are vying actively for the available traffic . .. the consequences of this evolutionary development in terms of growth in the systems' capacity, efficiency and conditions of service have been, as we have emphasized, of substantial benefit to the country as a whole.
I wish to submit, Mr. Speaker, that the four maritime provinces, through their transportation commissions, expressed similar sentiments, adding that competition between the different forms of transportation is highly desirable. The trucking industry, therefore,

should be considered with the other types of transportation media as the instruments of national policy. The proof of the importance of modern motor transport is found in the entrance of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways into the trucking industry. They are now in it in a big way, having purchased two of the largest truck lines in Canada doing business from coast to coast.
All this bill provides is the right of appeal to the board against any discriminatory rates, and the right to be heard in open court. I am particularly keen on the passage of this bill because the lakehead cities of Fort William and Port Arthur are approximately 850 or 900 miles from Toronto and 420 miles from Winnipeg. As a result of the distance between the heavier centres of population, we have never received due consideration from the railways in so far as fair freight rates are concerned. I can give an example of this discrimination. The freight rate on canned goods shipped from Chatham, Ontario to Fort William is $1.57 per one hundred pounds. When a wholesaler in Fort William ships these canned goods to Geraldton or Marathon, there is a charge of $1.37 per one hundred pounds for a journey of approximately 200 miles. As I say, this came about as a result of the horizontal freight rate increases that occurred during the last ten years. It was this policy of horizontal rate increases which damaged our chances to compete with other parts of the country, and which worked to our considerable disadvantage in comparison with the eastern parts of the province of Ontario.
This unfair policy, which we hope the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation will remedy in due course, has had the effect of turning shippers to and from the lakehead to motor transport for some of their needs. It is because of these cogent reasons that northwestern Ontario has suffered more than its share from unbalanced freight rates which, directly or indirectly, everyone must pay. Higher freight costs, I submit, have a direct relationship with higher than average unemployment.
I think we should preserve the competitive spirit in Canadian transportation. The government should preserve competition as it battles cartels and combines. An independent trucking industry should be given an opportunity to compete and survive for the benefit of all Canadians. The passing of this bill will at least give the trucking industry a chance to speak and fight for itself, from which in the end no one would suffer but rather each would enjoy the fruit of his labour.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill is read for the second time, I should like to point out to hon. members some considerations which made me support this legislation. As did the hon. member who preceded me, I shall commend the mover of the bill, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) who, I think, is sincerely concerned in the trucking industry, as he, indeed, proved to be when a somewhat similar legislation was submitted-as he mentioned a few moments ago-i.e. when Bill C-33 was brought forward in the first half of this session and, as we may recall, was passed unanimously by the house.
I have no intention of repeating what other hon. members said before me about trucking, but, as they stressed, that industry is constantly gaining in importance in this country. It should therefore, to my mind, certainly have at least the opportunity of competing on equal terms with the National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway company.
I believe it has already been proved in various ways that the railway companies are competing unfairly with the truckers in Quebec and throughout Canada. I shall mainly deal with the matter with regard to the province of Quebec. Obviously, such competition sometimes puts the trucking industry in a somewhat precarious position. It is known that the National Railways are subsidized by the federal government, and that they use these amounts in a way prejudicial to the trucking industry, because the truckers have to face a heavier competition when the railways are resorting to what could be called unfair practices by lowering their rates below cost price.
We must not forget that truckers pay income tax, that they pay taxes and contribute their share to the federal treasury, and further that in the end that money is used to create difficulties for them.
Obviously others tell us that railways and railway employees also had to face competition from truckers especially in the last few years and since the first world war.
Now, this amendment proposed in Bill C-39 will enable each group, the trucking industry on the one hand and the railways on the other hand, amending as it does clause 334 of the Railway Act, to submit representations to the board of transport commissioners in order that their views may be to known.
I support the bill because it will permit free competition between the operators of the various means of transportation we have in this country.
I feel, as was pointed out by previous speakers, that we must protect the interests

Railway Act
of the general public in the whole country. Therefore, if some areas of the country have obtained rate reduction on account of the competition from truckers, I feel that it should be admitted that railway freight rates should not be set below cost and this in order that competition may be fair.
If the freight rates or the railway rates are below cost, they necessarily threaten the trucking companies already doing business in the country, and since the railways, and particularly the Canadian National Railways, have deficits and it is the government which pays those deficits, I feel that the situation is unfair for truckers.
Furthermore, I know that the trucking industry has already made representations to the federal government on that matter, as did the Quebec trucking industry which, last autumn, forwarded a brief to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) to set out its situation and even its opposition to any additional subsidy to the C.N.R.
All those questions are under consideration. Several have already been thoroughly dealt with by the government and others will be considered.
I therefore believe that it would be wise to pass this amendment so as to let the trucking industry put forward its views to the board of transport commissioners when they argue that the railways are competing with them in a discriminatory or dishonest way by abnormally cutting their transport rates.
For these reasons, I shall vote in favour of the bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take but a few minutes to say that I wholeheartedly support the bill introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) under which the trucking industry will have a right of appeal to the board of transport commissioners regarding charges agreed upon by the Canadian National Railways or other railway companies and the shippers.
What I know of the trucking industry, I know from the submissions that were sent to us by the Quebec trucking association, but I believe the problem is the same in the nine other provinces.
I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I had the opportunity in the past to discuss that matter with him, and I know that he has a thorough knowledge of this serious problem which, I can safely say, threatens our country's trucking industry.	,

As was pointed out by a previous speaker, we adopted in this house, not very long ago, a bill guaranteeing some fundamental freedoms in this country. I feel that if a decision is taken by such a responsible public agency as the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, those who might fear encroachment of their rights should be entitled to appeal before those who have rendered a decision.
The Quebec trucking association, through the medium of Mr. Camille Archambault, has submitted to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer), several briefs of which copies were circulated among us. In my opinion, it is time the government should take action in this particular field.
I do not want to be a hypocrite and say that I will vote in favour of the bill, because I strongly suspect that the question will never come to a vote. My only purpose in taking part in this debate is to make it clear to the government that there is a serious problem in the trucking industry and that it rests with the government to introduce in this house during the present session or the next, a bill to remedy the situation that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway dealt with so efficiently.
The trucking industry employs thousands of Canadians, and revenues of taxes levied from Canadians should not contribute to the ruin of several companies engaged in this type of business in our country. If the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada issues orders or gives rulings which are or could be prejudicial to the trucking industry, it seems to me that under the bill of rights we have adopted, the representatives of that industry should have the right to air their grievances before the board.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay our proceedings, but I would urge the government to take this problem into consideration once more, as it has undoubtedly done in the past, and to take concrete action either before the end of the current session or at the beginning of the next one.
