I trust*1 that the house will do the same with this bill, but I hope it will not meet the same

fate that seems to have overtaken Bill No. C-33 in the other place. It seems to be rather unfortunate that bills sponsored byprivate members of this house do not get very far in the other place. In spite of the unanimous support for Bill No. C-33-and the members of the opposition who spoke in favour of that bill have spoken in favour of Bill No. C-39-it still sits in committee in the other place and no one knows when it will be reported out of committee. This I think is the wrong way for the other place to treat legislation which has been passed by this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext: Order. I think I should intervene and remind the hon. member that it is not in order to criticize the actions of the other place.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will not criticize the actions of the other place. I will let them speak for themselves.
As I have said, the bill under discussion is a companion piece of Bill No. C-33. Bill No. C-33, which was referred to by the sponsor, gave the right to trucking associations under the Transport Act to appeal to the minister. This bill gives trucking associations the right to appeal to the board of transport commissioners. In the special committee on government owned railways, air lines and shipping, the president of the Canadian National more than once mentioned the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was an expert in this field of transportation so far as the trucking industry was concerned. I think that we who have listened not only to his explanation of and reason for this bill, but also to his explanation of his previous bill can well understand that he has done a great deal of research and study. I know myself that he attended hearings before the board of transport commissioners. He also attended hearings in the other place. This is not by way of criticism at all, but he did attend hearings in the other place when the previous bill was under study. The point which was made which impressed me tremendously was that the board of transport commissioners do hear briefs and representations from provincial governments. They will hear representations from individual shippers or from an organization of shippers but, under the present legislation, they will not hear briefs or representations from those people who are most affected, namely a competitive shipping medium.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway had mentioned the fact that those incentive rates have been as much as 75 per cent lower than previous agreed charges or previous statutory rates. It does appear to me that if there was that much profit in the carrying 90205-6-514i
Railway Act
of traffic-under the law the railways must not give an incentive rate or an agreed charge which is not compensatory; under the law the railways must make money on the rates they charge-if they could drop the rate 75 per cent, then we may ask how accurate is their costing, how accurate is their analysis of their own expenses. Perhaps they do not know what it costs to carry freight. As we were told in the special committee, a representative of the railway simply sits down with the manufacturer and agrees on a charge right across the board. This is fine. We are all for cheaper transportation in this country of tremendous distances, but we are not in favour of the elimination of competition because this will not bring cheap transportation. It will end in very expensive transportation charges.
There must be regulations. There must be regulation of the trucking industry in the same way as there is regulation of the railroads. It seems to me that the delegation of this responsibility to the individual public utility commissions of the ten provinces is not the proper way to regulate the trucking industry when you consider its importance in the over-all transportation scheme of this country. A change must be made, and it would be better if this change were made in the way of government legislation introduced to take care not only of the railways but of other forms of transportation as well. There should be a bill to amend the Railway Act or the Transport Act. It would be much better for the government to introduce this legislation and it would not bog down in the other place.
In regard to incentive rates, it seems to me there is a possibility that an argument might be made to bring in the bill of rights because the bill of rights refers to:
The right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law.
Certainly, a businessman operating a trucking business is operating his property, and if he has built up this business and then a government sponsored competitor goes to his customers and offers rates which are not compensatory but are offered with the idea of driving this man out of business, is it not a fact that he has been deprived of the enjoyment and the use of his property? This is the nub of the problem, whether the rates charged are compensatory. This is the point the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has made time after time. There is no guarantee that those incentive rates are compensatory. There can be no guarantee unless an investigation is made. As he pointed out, out of some 30,000 rates allowed over the last period of years not more than ten have been investigated.

Railway Act
Those were investigated only because complaints were made, but complaints cannot be made by the people who know best whether the rates are compensatory. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this bill will be of advantage to the railways themselves, because it is not doing the railway any service for the board of transport commissioners to agree to rates which will cause the railways to lose money, and in so doing also wreck a competitive business.
From our work on the special committee we know that over the last three years $5 million has been voted each year for the acquisition of truck lines by the Canadian National system. We do not know whether the prices paid were right. We do not know about the operations of these companies. We do not know how profitable they have been. We do know, mainly by reason of the work by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), that they have not been as successful under railway operation as they were under private operation. This may well change in the years to come, but there must be control and regulation. It comes down to that.
Ever since confederation we have had control and regulation of transportation costs whether the transportation has been by railway or is now by truck, pipe line, air freight or what have you. In this particular field we are Balkanized into ten different nations, ten different provinces, each with its own regulatory body and with no body governing interprovincial trade. It does seem to me that the hon. member has done a service to the house and to the country by bringing this condition to the attention of the house.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO TRANSPORT BOARD ON COMPETITIVE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to support strongly Bill No. C-39. I should like to read the provision because I think the operative words in the bill should be emphasized. They are:
If an association or other body representative of the motor vehicle operators of Canada or of a province thereof considers that a competitive rate has subjected the said operators to an undue, or unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage, the said association or other body may apply to the board-
I emphasize those words. The bill simply seeks the right for these people to apply to the board. It does not bind the board in any way to give a favourable decision. It simply gives a part of our private enterprise system the right of appeal against a discriminatory practice.
I do not think anybody in this house and possibly no Canadian would deny that Canada still needs its railways. We need them so much that we will not deny their very great need at this time for financial assistance from the public purse. When the rail-

ways first came into existence in Canada they performed a great service. They knit what was then raw, unsettled land into a great nation, a nation which will become greater. But surely in 1961, over 70 years later, there is a need for a wider and more diversified transportation industry and less of a need for the monopoly which the railways have enjoyed for all these many years.
We need our trucking industry. We need it more each day. Certainly in the province of Alberta, other western provinces and in in our new northern areas which are opening up the need for the trucking industry is as great today as was the need for railways 70 or 75 years ago. Surely then we should not deny them the right simply to apply to the board with regard to unfair or discriminatory practices. All the bill seeks is the right to apply to a board created by the federal government for a fair hearing and possible correction of what might be an unfair practice.
We in the west look at what the trucking industry has done. It has brought perhaps the greatest period of prosperity to Canada and certainly to the province of Alberta since 1946 and 1947 that we have ever enjoyed. It has brought to us and helped to maintain and expand our oil industry. Without the trucking industry we would have no oil industry as we know it today. We might have another Turner valley but not an oil industry which stretches from the United States border up into the Arctic islands. This industry has brought to western Canada and Canada generally enrichment of our economy and surely we should not deny those who are active in the industry the right to apply to one of our boards if they are being unfairly or unjustly treated.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) mentioned that there are 90,000 Canadians employed in the trucking industry. So far as their right to employment is concerned, surely they are entitled to this protection, the right to apply to the board if they are being discriminated against. Surely in this country, which we like to think is one of the freest in the western world, the right of monopoly should not be upheld.
In his introduction of the bill the hon. member also mentioned a trucking company which was acquired by the crown-owned railway. I should like to remind the house and particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) that some time before the summer recess I asked the minister a question which has not yet been answered. It had to do with East-West Transport Limited lowering its rates and being the greatest offender in the industry in lowering rates to what is probably an uneconomic level in

an endeavour to force upon Canadian business and the Canadian people a monopoly in the transportation industry.
As I say, this bill simply seeks the right to apply to the board of transport commissioners for protection of an industry that has been built up from an infant to a very efficient operation which is becoming larger all the time. The trucking industry is not asking for a monopoly. They are simply asking for the right to appeal against monopoly. May I call it six o'clock.

speechtext: I think that will be the arrangement for next week, the estimates of external affairs, national defence and privy council and, if they are completed, the Department of Defence Production.
